speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is my honour to present a petition pursuant to Standing Order 106 on behalf of a number of constituents. The petitioners are very concerned that the trade deal negotiated with the United States will have a fundamental impact on our ability as a country to pursue economic, cultural and political independence. The petitioners believe that the agreement will result in the loss of many, many jobs in various sectors of the economy as well as various regions of Canada. Therefore, they ask the Parliament of Canada to obtain a clear mandate from the Canadian people through a national debate on this issue during a national general election.

Mr. Speaker, I too have a petition that has been certified correct as to form pursuant to Standing Order 106. The petitioners are residents of the riding of Thunder Bay-Atikokan, particularly in the Westport area. They believe the trade deal would deny Canada the policy freedom to determine its own economic future and would undermine our ability to build a society distinct from that of the United States. The petitioners humbly pray and call upon Parliament to dissolve, and allow the people of Canada the opportunity to accept or reject the proposed trade agreement during a national general election.

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre H. Cadieux (Minister of Labour) moved
speechtext:
that Bill C-124, an Act to amend the Canada Labour Code, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I rise today to address the House concerning the Bill which I recently introduced which would make necessary changes to legislation dealing with the all important subject of occupational safety and health. These changes, while minor in themselves, will help make the Canada Labour Code a more flexible and efficient instrument for the protection of Canadian workers.
The first of these changes is a series of amendments to Part IV of the Code which have general application. The second relates only to the federally regulated coal mines in Cape Breton.

Mr. Speaker, as Minister of Labour I have always considered the promotion of occupational safety and health to be one of the most important tasks in my department's mandate. Mr. Speaker, I would ask Hon. Members on both sides of this House to co-operate in giving expeditious approval to the proposed amendments, for the sake of the working men and women whose lives and well-being depend to a large extent on the quality of the legislation we provide.

The over-all objective of this Bill is to ensure consistency between the recently amended Part IV of the Canada Labour Code and the regulations made pursuant to the Code.
[ Translation]
One major intent of the 1984 Code amendments had been to clarify the prime responsibility of the employer for employees' occupational safety and health. Mr. Speaker, the regulationmaking authorities of the Code in this respect were therefore limited to precise standards which could be rigidly prescribed.
April 26, 1988



This new approach has generally worked well, but some serious concerns regarding situations and environments in which some flexibility is required were raised during the drafting of the regulations. These concerns are again arising in the regulation revision process. The proposed amendments to the Code will resolve those concerns by providing new or clearer authorities.
For the sake of clarity I shall present the changes in logical order rather than in a clause-by-clause succession. First, I will deal with the amendments of general application.
Clauses 4 and 5 of the Bill will provide authority pursuant to the proposed Subsections 105(7), 106(1.1) and (1.2), to make regulations for circumstances or situations in which it is not possible to prescribe rigid standards.

For example, Mr. Speaker, it is sometimes impossible to make regulations that cover every aspect of an engineering work or structure. Such situations may best be covered by a requirement that the work or structure be constructed "in accordance with good engineering practice". A professional engineer can certify that good engineering practice has been used, but this is not a prescribed standard and such a requirement would not be permitted by the current authorities in the Code. The proposed amendment will permit such a requirement, but only where the Governor in Council deems it appropriate.

Authority is also required to permit regulations to be made applicable generally to all workplaces, or all classes of employment, or particularly to one or more workplaces or one or more classes of employment as may be specified in the regulations.

For example, it would be appropriate to require a higher level of lighting in a warehouse where explosives or toxic substances are being handled, compared to a similar warehouse in which no hazards are presented by the materials being handled.

To ensure that employees enjoy the protection offered by the most recent updated standards, authority is required to reference standards as amended from time to time. Authority is also required to use the words: "to the extent that it is practicable or reasonably practicable." This would cover situations where it was found that it would be unreasonable to prescribe one precise standard for all situations.

It would be unreasonable, for example, to expect that buildings built before 1985 would meet all the requirements of the 1985 Building Code. It would be more appropriate to write
Canada Labour Code
a regulation requiring that all buildings will comply with the most recent building code to the extent that it is reasonably praticable.
Referring to Clause 2 of the Bill, the proposed amendement would authorize the provision in the regulations that requires an annual report on each safety and health committee's activities to be made in the prescribed form to a person designated by the regulation. This would permit Fabour Canada to know whether the safety health committees are performing their prescribed functions effectively, or whether they might need assistance.

I will now address the proposed amendments that only refer to federally regulated coal mining in Cape Breton, Nova Scotia.
Because of the special risks involved in working in the Cape Breton Development Corporation's coal mines in Nova Scotia, it is proposed to establish a tripartite Coal Mining Safety Commission. The Commission would have the authority to review and approve plans, procedures, methods and equipment in order to ensure that they will be safe in the ever-changing mining environment.
The Commission would also have the authority to vary or exempt the application of regulations, or to substitute a different standard where such actions will provide equal or better safety protection for the coal miners.

Referring to Clause 3 of the Bill, the proposed Sections 94.1 and 94.2 of the Code would set out the manner of establishment, selection, and remuneration of Commission members and the powers and duties of the Commission.
Referring to Clause 1 of the Bill, the proposed Section 82.3 requires that the employer, the Cape Breton Development Corporation, shall comply with the conditions and provisions imposed by the Commission under the authority of proposed Section 94.1.
In addition, it is proposed that pursuant to Section 82.3 the Code provide authority for two long-standing practices. The first is the practice permitting persons selected by the coal mining employees to inspect all workplaces in a mine to ensure that they are safe in all respects; the second practice is that of searching persons going underground to ensure that none carry cigarettes, lighters, alcohol, or drugs into the hazardous and potentially explosive mine atmosphere.
Referring to Clause 6 of the Bill, finally, to ensure continuity of safe operation of the coal mines, it is proposed that preexisting exemptions and approvals issued in the interests of safety remain in force.

April 26, 1988
Canada Labour Code

Referring to Clause 7 of the Bill, Mr. Speaker, it is proposed that the sections of this Act to amend the Canada Labour Code come into force at different times, particularly to permit time for the establishment of the Coal Mining Safety Commission and avoid having to make certain provisions of the regulations again under the amended Act.

I should mention, Mr. Speaker, that these amendments have the support of the Cape Breton Development Corporation and its employees.
I would urge Members of the House to grant speedy passage to this Bill at all stages, which will make a significant contribution to the occupational safety and health of working men and women in the federal jurisdiction.

Mir. Jean-Robert Gauthier (Ottawa-Vanier): Mr. Speaker, I am speaking on Bill C-124, an Act to amend the Canada Labour Code, on behalf of my colleague and friend, the Liberal critic, the Hon. Member for Saint-Jacques (Mr. Guilbault), who is now away from the House on an emergency.
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this Bill is to make health and safety standards for work in coal mines more flexible and effective, if I understood correctly, while at the same time protecting workers in the coal mines.
We support this amendment and we can tell the Minister and the Government that they will receive the usual cooperation from the Opposition to give this Bill speedy passage.
I would still like to tell the House that there are two Members who are very interested in this Bill, namely the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Dingwall), who will want to speak to it because it affects him very closely in his riding, and also the Hon. Member for Cape Breton- The Sydneys (Mr. MacLellan), who asked me to say a few words on the Bill in order to explain and properly understand the initiative that the Government is proposing to us.
One of the main objectives of the amendments made to the Code in 1986 was to establish the employer's primary responsibility for employees' health and safety on the job. In this regard, the regulatory authorities have confined themselves to specifying the standards that must be rigorously prescribed.
In general, this has worked well. This new procedure has been well received. However, the relationship of the regulations has given rise to serious questions in situations and environments that require some flexibility.
The following amendments to this Bill deal adequately with these concerns.
I shall deal with this Bill C-124 in terms of principles, Mr. Speaker, and leave it to the legislative committee to study the amendments more closely and in detail.
Clauses 4 and 5 of the Bill give the power to make regulations under Subsections 105(7), 106(1.1) and 106(1.2) in circumstances or situations where it is not possible to prescribe
rigid standards. Under Subsection 106(4), the regulations may be applicable: (a) generally, to all workplaces and all classes of employment; (b) specifically, to one or more workplaces or one or more classes of employment, as will be specified in the regulations.
Furthermore, under Subsection 106(5) of the Canada Labour Code, a standard may be incorporated by reference to other standards and may be amended as these are amended from time to time. Under this provision, employees will be able to enjoy the protection afforded by the latest updated health and safety standards, while it also obviates the need for amending the regulations.
Under new Subsection 106(6), the terms "practicable" and "reasonably practicable" may be incorporated.
Mr. Speaker, it is generally recognized, and I think everyone in the industry will agree, that it is unreasonable to prescribe a single specific standard in every case. There are exceptions where one must be flexible, and, as the Minister remarked, we must be flexible in applying these regulations. The Committee will have to examine these conditions and further clarify the purpose of this provision.
Clause 2 of this Bill concerns the authority under paragraph 92(1 l)(f) to require safety and health committees to submit an annual report. I think this provision is reasonable and acceptable, if we want Labour Canada to know exactly what is going on, whether the safety and health committees are effective in performing their prescribed duties and whether they need assistance.
The amendments in Bill C-124 concerning the coal mines of the Cape Breton Development Corporation are quite straightforward, and 1 think the Minister has explained quite clearly why, in these specific situations where the federal Government is practically the sole authority with respect to management and health and safety concerns, the Bill proposes to establish a tripartite Coal Mining Safety Commission that will have the authority to examine and approve plans, procedures, methods and equipment, to ensure they do not present any hazards in this fast developing mining industry.
The Commission will also have the authority to amend the regulations, to suspend their application and to substitute certain standards for other standards, provided they offer the same or better safeguards for coal miners.
Clause 3, which is new, will establish a new agency, Mr. Speaker, the Coal Mining Safety Commission, responsible mainly for approving, as appropriate, plans and procedures to be followed in coal mines and mining methods, machinery and equipment for use in coal mines, and they also exempt coal mines from certain regulations of general application.
We welcome this provision as well, but the "notwithstanding" provisions that follow are somewhat puzzling. Take, for instance, Subsection 94.2 (2). I will read it to you, Mr. Speaker.
April 26, 1988

On the application of an employer, the Commission or a person designated
by the Commission for the purposes of this subsection may, where, in the
opinion of the Commission or that person, protection of the safety and health
of employees would not thereby be diminished,
(>a) approve in writing the use by the employer in coal mines of mining methods, machinery or equipment in respect of which no prescribed safety standards are applicable;
We would like to ask the Minister for explanations, maybe in committee, on these provisions granting exemptions in order to clarify their scope and perhaps better understand the objective sought.
Mr. Speaker, as I was just saying, we intend to support this Bill and to make it conform as soon as possible to the desire to make the regulation somewhat more flexible while keeping in mind our responsibilities for health and safety.
The comments I have to make on that, I think, are fairly supportive, I would say, of this Bill, and as I was just saying, we will give it our approval as soon as possible on second reading so that in committee, my colleagues from the House, and especially those in my Caucus from the Cape Breton region, can certainly make amendments, if necessary.

Mr. Speaker, it is with pleasure that I rise to speak on the motion for the second reading of Bill C-124, an Act to amend the Canada Labour Code. The provisions of Bill C-124 represent an important step forward in terms of health and safety in the workplace generally, and in the coal mining industry in particular. I wish to commend the Minister of Labour (Mr. Cadieux) for the extensive consultation he undertook in the preparation of this Bill. I understand that he put in place an elaborate ongoing consultative process with the coal mining industry, with the officials of the Cape Breton Development Corporation, with the United Mine Workers, and with the Canadian Labour Congress. His efforts in that regard represent a remarkable precedent in terms of government and labour and industry working together to bring about improvements to the Canada Labour Code in respect of health and safety in the workplace.
Unions throughout this country and internationally have been vociferous in bringing forth their proposals to increase the level of health and safety in industry generally, and in the mining sector in particular. We in Canada have experienced a number of great disasters associated with the mining industry. We all recall only too well the Springhill mine disaster, where an underground explosion led to a number of fatalities.
The mining industry, by its very nature, presents a number of dangers, not the least of which is the lack of access to immediate escape and immediate emergency equipment. Certainly, it is a sector which presents a unique set of circumstances.
It is appropriate that Bill C-124 is before the House this week for debate, given that April 28 has been designated a day of mourning for all those killed or injured in the workplace. This day of commemoration is sponsored by the Canadian
Canada Labour Code
Labour Congress, the idea being to bring to the attention of the public the need for increased health and safety in the workplace. A number of district labour councils throughout the country, along with a number of municipalities, have joined in proclaiming April 28 as a day of mourning, in recognition of those killed or injured in the course of their employment.
There are far too many accidents in the workplace, leading to serious injury and death. We are always, we hope, moving forward in the area of health and safety in the workplace, and those involved in promoting health and safety in the workplace deserve the commendation of this House for their efforts in keeping before the public and lawmakers the need for increased health and safety in the workplace.
As a labour lawyer and one who has been involved in a number of cases involving health and safety aspects in the workplace, I can tell you that it is an area that presents the employee with some very difficult decisions. Often, an employee is required, as part of his contract of employment, to undertake dangerous work, and if at any time the employee chooses not to undertake the work requested, that employee risks being the subject of disciplinary action on the part of the employer, including the potential loss of employment. As a result, the employee generally has little if any control over working conditions.
Bill C-124 goes some distance in correcting that situation in so far as the mining sector is concerned, in as much as employees would have an important role, through the Coal Mining Safety Commission, in ensuring control over the health and safety standards to be followed. To my mind, this is an important forward step, and one which gives the employee important input in terms of the health and safety standards to be followed.
Given the level of technology and equipment utilized in the mining sector, one could not expect the miners to be totally familiar with its dangers. Through the Coal Mining Safety Commission, the employees will now have access to the kind of expertise and knowledge necessary to ensure that the new equipment is not introduced into the mine without assurances that the equipment is in fact safe for use, with the necessary safety practices and regulations already in place.
In the event that a given piece of equipment is not deemed to be dangerous in and of itself, or involved in a dangerous aspect of mining, it may be that there will be no necessity for having standards and regulations in place in respect of its use. 1 commend the Minister for the extensive consultations that have taken place in bringing this Commission forward. We have had accidents in Cape Breton. We had a recent most serious fire in a Cape Breton coal mine which caused a close down. Safety in the mining industry is something that ought to be and is, I am sure, foremost in the minds of those working in the mines and in the minds of their families. It is a dangerous occupation, and concern for safety is always uppermost in the minds of the families.

April 26, 1988
Canada Labour Code
I support the Bill in principle at second reading stage. It moves forward in bringing into line some of the technical regulations with the new changes to the Canada Labour Code, and it is important that this Bill be given speedy passage in the House.
I do, however, want to speak about a reservation I have concerning the provisions in Clause 1 of the Bill which will add a section following Section 82.2 of the Canada Labour Code. It will put into law a provision requiring a search of those entering a mining area who are not employed there. Every person will be searched, and a proportion of employees working in the underground portion of the mine will have to submit to personal searches conducted in a manner to be prescribed by the regulations.
I understand from discussions with the Minister and his staff that this provision in the Bill, even though it is written as a law of general application, refers only to coal miners. Under the Constitution, of course, the only coal mining activity undertaken under federal jurisdiction is that of the federal Crown corporation, DEVCO. I understand it is still a federal Crown corporation but I do not know what plans the Government may have for the future. The only coal mining activity affected by this particular provision will be the coal mines in Cape Breton.
I do understand, as the Minister indicated in his speech, that there was consultation with representatives of the employees. There is a proposal to search to make sure that matches, cigarette lighters and these types of things are not brought into the mine even accidentally by an employee who is perhaps forgetful or puts on different clothing which happens to have matches, cigarette lighters or whatever in the pockets. This employee may, without thinking while in the mine, "flick his Bic", I think it is said sometimes. I have seen people do that without thinking. It does not sound like a very diabolical provision if it is designed to prevent an accident from occurring. However, I do have a grave reservation about including in a law of general application the requirement to search. This may establish a precedent for all sorts of other types of search and seizure provisions which may well be opposed by many segments of the society for reasons of invasion of privacy, civil liberties and for a further moving of the state in the direction of denying individual liberties.
I would, of course, underline the importance of safety in coal mines. An explosion would be devastating. We all know of the famous Davey lamps and other lamps that have been devised to provide light underground in coal mines without causing explosions. I have grave reservations about including this particular phraseology in a law which appears to be of general application, although we heard today that it only has application to the Cape Breton coal mine because that is the only coal mine under federal jurisdiction. Having said that, I will be having further discussions with the Minister as to what the consequences of this search provision are.
I wanted to express those reservations at second reading stage but at the same time support in principle the legislation contained in Bill C-124 together with the various provisions which provide for a major improvement in access to employees, access to inspection procedures underground, access that employees will now have through the Coal Mining Safety Commission to information, technical knowledge and understanding of exactly what is going on concerning health and safety and the opportunity to examine and to put in place safe work practices with respect to new equipment which may be brought into mining activity. All of those things are very progressive actions and put the employees in a position of being able to have control over their workplace where they daily take great risks.
The other provision in Clause 2 of requiring health and safety committees to submit annual reports of their activities appears to be a minor clause in the Bill before us today, but it is a very important one. It allows the monitoring of the activities of these committees and allows health and safety committees to bring to the attention of officialdom, if you will, activities which they have undertaken during the year and to point out any serious problems encountered. These can be put on the record so they will not be forgotten and action can be taken. If not, someone can point to the very serious problems in the current annual report or the following one. A watch-dog can be provided, as it were, to make sure that the committee reports are part of the public record and will be acted upon.
1 commend and thank the Minister for bringing this legislation forward. I reiterate the support of our Party in the House for Bill C-124 in principle with the reservations that I have expressed.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to join with my colleagues in opposition expressing my gratitude, if you will, to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Cadieux) who has obviously, and I say so with respect, taken a great interest in the subject matter before us. We are aware of many of the activities of his predecessors who have also had as their goal the improvement of occupational safety and health as it affects employees and businesses across Canada.
Since the Bill does zero in on a particular Crown corporation which is of great interest to me and the people I represent, I would also like to pay due respect to the union representatives of the United Mine Workers of America, and in particular, their safety co-ordinator in the person of Mr. Paul MacNeil, and of course representatives of the Cape Breton Development Corporation who represented the employer in the consultation process. Regarding the substantive parts of the Bill, I say to the Minister that I understand, appreciate and concur with the intent of Bill C-124. However, I have a number of reservations and qualifications that I will want to pursue at another time with the Minister as well as with representatives of the union and with management.
April 26, 1988

I do wish to say now at second reading stage that safety in the coal mining industry in Cape Breton has been of primary concern not only to me but indeed to my own predecessors who have served in this Chamber on previous occasions. It was through our efforts that many good things have come about for safety and occupational health in the coal mines.
Some of these amendments may appear at first instance to be rather minor in their substantive effect on coal mining in Cape Breton. However, they are certainly substantial in the effect they will have on the industry. To be fair to the Minister, I think he is very much aware of that and has responded to the representations of union and management. I wish to compliment him for responding so quickly and so efficiently on their behalf.
The legislation contains provision for a tripartite commission. The Minister will know that in setting up this commission, much of the discretionary authority still remains with the Governor in Council. Although I can understand and appreciate the need for flexibility in the implementation of agreed upon standards, we must be cognizant of the need to make certain that the agreement on a standard and the implementation of a standard may be two different things.
Let me make the point that standards have to be very clear to management and to union representatives as well as to the working person. Everyone must understand beyond a shadow of a doubt what is being talked about. There can, however, be some grey areas, as I think the Minister has indicated in his remarks, for which their must be flexibility in the implementation of a particular standard. I can appreciate the Minister's comments on that as well as those of my colleague from the New Democratic Party.
With the intent of the Bill being the improvement of occupational health and safety in the coal mines, I would hope that the upgrading of a standard would be the over-all objective rather than the relaxation of a standard. I would hope that there would always be a desire, both directly and indirectly, to try to improve upon that standard so that we can ensure the employees, their supervisors, the management, family members and the community at large that safety is the number one objective in this process.
That leads me to the issue of regulations. I will be discussing with the Minister and I am discussing with members of the union regulations for coal dust levels. I believe the Minister is aware that union representatives would prefer to have a level of four as opposed to the regulated level of six. It is my understanding from the representatives that there is a clear desire and intention to move to the level of four. I just bring that to the attention of Hon. Members opposite to underline the significance and importance of the intent of this aspect of the Bill.
Under the Bill, much of the discretionary authority still lies with the Governor in Council. The Commission is to consist of five individuals. The Minister said that he would appoint the chairman, and four other individuals would be appointed, being equally representative of non-supervisory employees and
Canada Labour Code
employers at DEVCO. I would hope that the union will have a real say in the determination of who those appointees will be and not simply be used, and I am certain the union will not simply be used by this Minister.
I give the Minister notice now that I will be asking him at a subsequent time what the prescribed budget of the particular Commission will be and what sort of actual assistance will be made available to the Commission. I will ask specific questions about the rules of natural justice and how they will be applicable. I will also ask questions about further developments in the coal mining industry of Cape Breton and what role he envisages this Commission to play and how it will interact with other agencies of both federal and provincial Governments. Those are questions which are rather fundamental to these amendments which, at the outset, may appear to be minor. However, in many instances, they would have a substantive impact on the coal mining industry of Cape Breton.
In addition to the number of individuals on the Commission, and I hope the Minister will provide detail on that at a later time, the regulations the Commission will be making are extremely important. It is extremely important that the Commission have broad consultation among the representatives of the union and that it continuously try to improve upon the standards in order to try to optimize as best as humanly possible the occupational health and safety of the workers who are employed at the Cape Breton Development Corporation.
In the Minister's speech, he said that it is proposed that pursuant to Section 82(3) the Code will provide authority for two long-standing practices. It is the second practice that I wish to draw to your attention, Mr. Speaker. He said that the second practice is that of searching persons going underground to ensure that none carry cigarettes, lighters, alcohol or drugs into the hazardous, potentially explosive mine atmosphere.
If one were to read those sentences in isolation, I think one could argue that that is search and seizure. 1 will want the Minister to qualify that on the record at a later date. I wish to know what the intent of that really is. I also wish to review very carefully the wording of that practice.
1 am sure that the Minister is not suggesting that there be a pre-test for everyone and anyone who works at a particular mine site. I think he is suggesting something much less than that. However, the intent is very important when achieving the particular objective.
There are a number of concerns I have that I am sure can be dealt with in a semi-private atmosphere along with my NDP colleagues to the left. I am sure that we can resolve these and some of the other points that I have raised with the Minister. However, 1 would like to have some further explanation of some of the interpretation of the wording given by the Department and the Minister. My colleague from Cape Breton-The Sydneys also wants that information because he has coal mines in his constituency as well and has been following the subject of occupational health and safety as much as I have over the last number of years.

April 26, 1988
Canadian Environmental Protection Act
Finally, I wish to reiterate that I think the Minister has accepted the challenge made by representatives of the United Mine Workers of America, in particular Mr. Paul MacNeil. I am sure he would have been in Ottawa today to answer any questions any Member had but he has been ill for a number of weeks, like I have, and I thank you for the flowers you sent, Mr. Speaker.
I will conclude by saying that we want to have another look at some of the questions I have raised before giving swift passage to this Bill.

speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Vezina (for the Minister of the Environment) moved
speechtext: that Bill C-74, an Act respecting the protection of the environment and of human life and health, be read the third time and passed.

Mr. Speaker, I am very proud to speak on the Canadian Environmental Protection Act, before you today for third reading. I am proud that we are meeting the commitment of the October, 1986, Throne Speech. And I am proud because this is the first piece of comprehensive, federal environmental protection legislation in the history of our country.
I wish, at this time, to echo the words of the chairman of the legislative committee that tabled its amendments on Bill C-74 in this House on March 23, 1988. The work of the committee was indeed a superb non-partisan exercise, where all worked together without regard to political affiliation to make this the best possible legislation for Canada.
I wish to spend the next few minutes describing the amendments brought by the committee that are among the highlights of Bill C-74.
The definition of "substance" in Clause 3 has been adjusted, so that it now clearly applies not only to matter that is capable of being dispersed in the environment, or of being transformed and then dispersed in the environment, but also to matter capable of causing such transformation. This will enable us to
regulate substances strictly based on their ability to transform other matter and to cause its dispersal.
For the first time in a federal statute, "biotechnology" is defined, and the revamped definition of the term "release" in Clause 3 now specifically covers discharge, spray, injection, inoculation and abandonment of any substance governed by the Act.
We have not forgotten that the provinces are partners in the fight to protect Canada's environment. Clause 6 of the new statute forges new links to make that effort more effective and productive. Under that part, a federal-provincial committee will be created to advise on regulations on the release or disposal of substances, as well as their storage, display, handling and transport. The committee may also advise on any other matter related to the administration of the Act.
These links will be further enhanced by the concept of "equivalency" now contained in the statute. We recognize provincial strength and expertise in such areas as control of emissions, effluents, and waste disposal. The Canadian Environmental Protection Act will enable the Governor in Council, on the recommendation of the Minister of the Environment to recognize provincial regulations as equivalent to those under the federal Act.
This will ensure that both jurisdictions co-operate in the management of toxic substances from cradle to grave, without duplication or overlap. The same concept of "equivalency" through an Order in Council is provided in Part V of the statute covering international air pollution. However, there will still be accountability. The Minister of the Environment must report annually to this House on the administration and enforcement of the Act, including an accounting of the enforcement of equivalent provincial measures.
The clauses of Bill C-74 dealing with disclosure of information have been totally overhauled, and are now in harmony with the federal Access to Information and Workplace Hazardous Materials Information Review Acts.
We have also dealt with two concerns expressed during the development of the legislation. First, the Canadian Environmental Protection Act now automatically bans the export of substances prohibited for use in Canada, except for disposal purposes. Second, there must now be notification, by the polluter, to members of the public who may be adversely affected by the unauthorized release, spill, leak, et cetera, of a substance. This requirement exists in Part IV of Bill C-74 as obligating federal departments, agencies, boards, and Crown corporations to provide the same notification.



y
April 26, 1988

I am pleased that the concern of the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) that federal departments, agencies, board and Crown corporations must not be above the law when the environment is at stake, did not go unheeded by the legislative committee in its clause-by-clause review of Bill C-74. Amendments to the Canadian Environmental Protection Act now ensure that there will be no doubt on this matter.
The federal Government and its agencies intend to be exemplary in complying with the new legislation. Clause 4 of the Bill states that the statute is "binding on Her Majesty in Right of Canada". However, the amended clauses of the Bill dealing with federal works, undertakings, lands, departments, boards, and agencies now go still farther. They now empower the Governor in Council, on the recommendation of the Minister of the Environment, to make regulations setting limits for the release of emissions and effluents by federal departments, boards and agencies, as well as by Crown corporations. Waste handling and disposal can also be regulated.
These clauses further require that if a harmful substance has been released into the environment, the responsible federal body must report the unauthorized release to an inspector or other designated person. The body or agency must then take all reasonable emergency measures to prevent danger to the environment, human life or health, and, as I mentioned previously, notify members of the public who may be adversely affected. It is specifically stated that inspectors have the right of access and entry to federal property, and may take emergency measures themselves if the relevant department, board, agency or Crown corporation does not do so.
One particularly significant aspect of the new statute is the extent of public participation assured by the legislation. The Act invites Canadians to participate in its administration. They can request the Minister to include a substance on the priority substances list for immediate assessment and investigation to determine its toxicity. They can register their objection to non-inclusion of a substance on the toxic substances list, and request a board of review. They can comment on regulations upon their publication in Part I of The Canada Gazette, or protest the Minister's decision not to regulate, again requesting a board of review. This opportunity for comment and objection extends equally to provisions of the statute that allow the granting, revocation, suspension or alteration of permits for disposal at sea.
One aspect of public involvement is already at work. The Priority Substances Advisory Panel, chaired by Dr. Ross Hume Hall of McMaster University and including provincial Government, industry, academic and environmental group representatives, is completing its rigorous analysis of candidate substances, leading to a short list of 50 substances for priority assessment and investigation of their environmental and health effects.
The authority of a board of review to award costs to interveners has been expanded. Now the board may grant interim travel, and other administrative costs to interveners
Canadian Environmental Protection Act
during the course of hearings and deliberations rather than solely at the conclusion of the board's work.
Also, for the first time in a federal environmental protection statute, two adult residents of Canada as individuals can petition the Minister to investigate a suspected violation. The Minister is then obliged to report his findings. In addition, private citizens who suffer, or may potentially suffer, loss or damage due to an offence committed under the Act can seek an injunction to prevent or stop the unlawful activity. Upon conviction of an offender they can seek a court order compensating them for their loss. They may also seek restitution through a civil suit.
It is in these ways that the Canadian Environmental Protection Act allows ordinary Canadians to become partners with the Government in the administration and enforcement of this statute which is designed to achieve the level of environmental protection, on a nation-wide basis, that they demand and deserve.
The Bill now before you is not solely the creation of lawyers, officials, and politicians working in isolation. This legislation is perhaps the most democratically devised statute to be considered by a federal Government in Canada. The process leading to the new Act really began in 1982 with the Environment Canada-Industry Workshop on New Chemicals.
The next vital steps were the reports of the Environmental Contaminants Act Amendments Consultative Committee, the Multi-Stakeholder Task Force on Management of Chemicals, and the government-industry study group that examined the aftermath of the Bhopal disaster and recommended how to avoid such an occurrence in Canada. These formed the basis of the draft Environmental Protection Act that the Minister of the Environment tabled in this House for discussion and consultation 16 months ago.
That tabling launched further consultations which actually lasted until late spring, 1987. When, as required by a new provision of the Act, Parliament reviews this statute in five years time, consultation may well begin again. It may seem to some that the consultation process is endless, but we are the better for it. Every sector of Canadian society was able to have its say. We received numerous letters and briefs and heard oral presentations.
We are fortunate that all the members of the legislative committee appointed to carry out clause-by-clause review were conscientious and zealous in their task. We took to heart the invitation by the Minister of the Environment to improve the Canadian Environmental Protection Act where we saw deficiencies. We, as well as the Minister, want the best, most comprehensive federal environmental protection legislation possible. I wish to thank my colleagues for their excellent work over these past weeks. We heard 36 witnesses and considered over 260 amendments, of which 142 were approved.

April 26, 1988
Canadian Environmental Protection Act
In conclusion, the Government has responded to the concern of Canadians for the protection of their environment. We have received their letters and read and heeded their representations. The Environmental Monitor report of last September further confirms results of surveys done over the past four years and tells us that 65 per cent of Canadians believe that environmental pollution has increased over the last five years. Seven in 10 Canadians believe that governments usually side with the industries that pollute rather than the affected public.
Passage of the Canadian Environmental Protection Act by this House will lay to rest that statement. It will show Canadians that we are committed to legislation that will protect our environment today and will serve us into the 21st century.

Mr. Speaker, it would be quite in order at this stage to thank the Hon. Member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers) for reading his prepared speech so well. In less than 10 minutes he has dealt with the subject matter, the complexity of which is mind-boggling, which has been before this House and in committee for over a year and a half. As he said, it has been the subject of public consultations, albeit very partial and very limited.
He has spoken at third reading without any indication of where the Parliamentary Secretary or the Minister himself are at this very important stage. We have not heard a speech by the Minister on Bill C-74 at second reading, at report stage, or today when it is customary for a Minister to launch the Bill in its final stage with an analysis of it which one would hope would bring out the positive features as well as the negative ones, the difficulties encountered, and the points which may still have to be resolved as experience is gathered.
The only political point made by the Member for Red Deer was at the end of his remarks when he proclaimed that this Bill will demonstrate that the Government does not side with industry. What a negative way of putting it, as if there would be a preoccupation with disclaiming that potential accusation. He was obviously motivated either by a guilt feeling or some other reason to say: "Don't you worry, the Government, contrary to impressions perhaps, does not side with industry".
The history of this Bill is rather peculiar. It had a tremendously flashy beginning and a weak finish, arriving at the finish line with barely any strength left in the system as demonstrated by the pathetic exchanges which took place last Tuesday and Wednesday at report stage.
I submit that the history of this Bill is one of retreats and reversals. It is very unfortunate that the Member for Red Deer could not find the time to dwell on that, let alone to put up a defence for the reversals, or possibly a defence for the retreats. However, that is the history of this Bill. It was proclaimed as the greatest invention since sliced bread. However, the ending of that particular initiative is pretty weak, to say the least. That applies not only to the substance of the Bill but also to the process, and I will elaborate on that in due course.
This Bill was proclaimed by the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) as the greatest legislation in the western
hemisphere. When we came to the end of the process the same Minister, descending to earth, admitted that it was one small step. Somehow I was sympathetic when he said that because it was a realistic and honest way to put it. It is one small step. In that sense, it is a step that can only be welcomed. However, I submit that despite the claim made at the conclusion of the speech of the Hon. Member for Red Deer this Bill could have been much stronger, as it was conceived in its original form when the consultations to which the Hon. Member referred were launched. The fact is that as time went on, the Bill was the object of erosion and attack, and in the end the Minister himself had to admit that it turned out to be a small step. But it could have been a stronger piece of legislation, and I will take the necessary time to elaborate on that.
The Minister claimed that this Bill would clean up the environment. The Hon. Member must have heard the Minister saying that in the House in Question Period. The Minister said the St. Clair River blob would be cleaned up. When visiting Halifax, the Minister claimed this Bill might be used to clean the Halifax Harbour and other trouble spots across the nation. Unfortunately, that is not to be the case. The measure now before us offers only a modest step with very little teeth, and those were gradually pulled out as the process advanced. I will touch on that later.
The Hon. Member for Red Deer made reference to consultations. Consultations did take place with the public, and that process of consultation on the draft Bill was completed. Then it came to the provinces and as a result of changes that were made which profoundly affected the thrust and impact of the Bill, the public was no longer the interlocutory of negotiations, nor were the non-governmental groups, the NGOs. As time progressed, we had a selective and restrictive consultation that became narrower and narrower in scope. I must say that in reply to the speech of the Hon. Member for Red Deer, for whom I have the highest esteem, because it has to be put on record.
As this Bill progressed there were some very interesting claims. There was the claim that the federal Government would not wait for the provinces to take action on the environment. "We are going to do it", said the Minister. In June 1987, the obligation was recognized to consult with the provinces before making regulations. In November of 1987, it was no longer an obligation. Then in March of this year the obligation was back. Each time the change was eloquently defended by the Government so that with respect to the obligation to consult we had a flip, a flop and a flip.
The progress of this Bill has been followed quite closely, as it should, by the media. It is interesting to note that on Sunday, August 16 of last year, The Toronto Star devoted a lead editorial to this Bill under the heading of "Meech Lake Blight Hits the Pollution Bill". It is worth reading. I will not read it into the record because it would take too long.
April 26, 1988

It begins by making the point that since the Progressive Conservative Party took office there have been worrisome signs that Ottawa may be ceding more turf to the provinces. Those were prophetic words. It was worrisome because the fight against pollution has to be nation-wide and, therefore, requires uniform leadership and standards that only Ottawa can establish. This delicate balance between Ottawa and the provinces was already put in danger, or at least upset, when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) in November of 1984 chopped $46 million from the budget of Environment Canada. People must be reminded of what happened and that it was done by the great defenders of the environment on the government side. Two months in office and the Government chopped $46 million from Environment Canada and then proceeded with consultations on this Bill.
In the end we have a consultative process that is mandatory, which means the Minister of the Environment must consult with all the provinces before regulations are drafted or emergency orders are issued to control toxic chemicals. It must be said in all fairness that Ottawa would retain the right to act on its own after consultations. The provisions in this Bill invite Ottawa to take the weakest possible action in order that everyone will agree, and that is usually the outcome of such consultations.
In order to understand this Bill we have to examine it, to begin with, from a constitutional point of view. How does the Constitution relate to the environment and vice versa? That aspect at third reading of this Bill is essential because it gives us an insight into the federal role in the environment. As a result of the consultation process with the provinces, the Bill has been weakened and it need not have been weakened. It is important, therefore, to put on record which constitutional experts came to speak on Bill C-74, and what they said.
I refer, first of all, to a lawyer in Calgary, Alastair Lucas. He wrote in the fall, 1987, issue of Resources, when commenting on the question of equivalency, to which the Hon. Member for Red Deer made reference in his speech, that an acceptable definition of equivalency may prove elusive in any event. Yet equivalency has become the main concept which finds its own way through this Bill as it relates to the federal role in applying this Bill.
He states also that the federal Government does not wish to see its environmental protection Act initiative end with an Act that has only patchwork effects nationally and then may be of little or no significance in some provinces. Unfortunately, that is exactly what this Bill has achieved.
What Alastair Lucas was urging should not happen from a constitutional point of view has happened. We have equivalency in the Bill, and we are heading for a patchwork Canada in the implementation of environmental protection.
It might be said, incidentally, that Alastair Lucas is the Acting Executive Director of the Canadian Institute of
Canadian Environmental Protection Act
Resources Law. He cannot be accused of being a supporter of the Liberal Party or a committed rabid environmentalist.
Is he alone in that viewpoint? Maybe it is just some might say a western aberration, something that comes out of a lonely guy in Calgary, someone who perhaps is frustrated because he does not get the recognition that he would like to receive. He is not alone. He is in some interesting company, I must say.
For instance, I bring to the attention of the House what was said on behalf of the Environmental Law Centre which is located in Edmonton by Elizabeth Swanson in her appearance before our committee which examined this Bill on December 10 of last year. She said: "I think the federal Government can consult its heart out with the provinces if it would like to do so". She stated that she really objected to this being a mandatory requirement to ministerial action, which she considers to be well within the competency of the federal Minister. She stated: "It seems to me in a way to be a political agreement taking the form of legislation". She was dead on in that. It was not a technical constitutional decision, it was a political decision. It was the emanation of the Meech Lake virus that found its way into Bill C-74.
She concluded by stating, as her colleague mentioned: "We do not object to the concept of the notion of co-operative federalism". Nobody does, of course not. It is the essence of our country. However, she stated, she has a little bit of difficulty when it starts popping up in our legislation.
It may be worth while to quote a voice from Toronto, the voice of Toby Vigod of the Canadian Environmental Law Association. She stated: "It has been our contention that the Minister of the Environment has been getting extremely conservative advice from the Department of Justice on federal constitutional authority to protect the environment". This is what she said in committee on January 19, 1988. She went on to urge the committee to obtain a written opinion from the Department of Justice on this issue. We tried. She said that such an opinion would then be subject to scrutiny by the committee, constitutional experts and the national legal environmental community at large. She said that in their opinion there is clear authority for the federal Government to take a strong role in environmental protection. There is, something which we argued in committee.
"Key constitutional heads of power are criminal law, trade and commerce and peace, order and good government," Professor Paul Emond wrote 15 years ago on the case for a strong federal role in environmental protection. He said that the constitutionality of a strong federal role in the environmental protection field is indisputable. Similarly, the arguments in favour of immediate federal action in this area are compelling. He said that what is needed now is for the federal Government to recognize this fact and to take the initiative in designing and implementing a comprehensive pollution control plan that will make a real contribution to improving our national environment.

April 26, 1988
Canadian Environmental Protection Act
Toby Vigod of CELA went on to say that the Environmental Protection Act as currently worded does not take the initiative. She pointed out that the Minister has brought forward new amendments that will provide that federal regulations may not apply if equivalent provisions are enforced in a province. She states that they have reviewed the submissions filed by the Alberta Environmental Law Centre and share their concerns regarding these new amendments. Thus there is a viewpoint in the West and a viewpoint in the East.
"Besides being rather unwieldy in terms of determining what constitutes equivalency," she said, "we are concerned that, again, there appears to be a deliberate attempt by the Government not to regulate in the area of toxic chemicals." She went on to point out that federal law should not be applied in a patchwork fashion. As well, there is a real constitutional argument that federal facilities operating in provinces with only so-called provincial equivalent regulations will totally be exempt from regulations. That is a big sore point that will come up later in my intervention.
She concluded by giving an example to which 1 would like to refer. She said that a federal facility in Ontario emitting a toxic chemical in excess of Ontario's equivalent regulations could argue, if charged with a breach of such regulations, that it is immune from the application of provincial laws because it is a federal facility. A much better course is to have strong minimum national standards and to then let the provinces enact stricter regulations where they feel it is appropriate. She went on to make specific suggestions.
It is a matter of great concern in the environmental community, and I suppose that this community embraces everybody who is concerned about our health, our natural resources, and the long-term interest of our economy, that here the Government made the wrong turn, the wrong decision.
Miss Vigod concluded by saying: "I think that in the area of environment public opinion is behind a strong national role". These are prophetic words of four months ago, because a few days ago we saw a poll confirming that.
Miss Vigod went on to say: "I think we should see it tested in the courts. We have seen the other happen: the provinces have tested their law and seen federal entities have charges dismissed on the basis of Crown immunity". That is the danger. She urged: "Let us try having strong federal law and take that challenge in the courts. I think it is time to put our money where our mouth is and I think the public and the courts are slowly becoming more attuned to environmental issues", which is another very sound political observation.
Miss Vigod, on behalf of CELA, further said: "Certainly when we appear in court now we get a far better hearing than we did 10 or 15 years ago. I think those issues are of national concern. In the area of toxic chemical law we have these other
features. Air pollutants and water pollutants do not respect provincial boundaries, and they are causing significant economic and environmental damage in this country".
She concluded by saying: "I say let us take that challenge. If it is struck down, then either we will be able to redefine how we will enact the role or the pressure really will come to bear on the provinces. There has always been a bit of jurisdictional buck passing. I think the time for federal standards is now. This is why we have also recommended that the power to enact standards be put specifically in this legislation". Several of us tried in the subsequent committee hearings, without succeeding.
Let me quote what was stated by another constitutional lawyer, lan Blue from Toronto, and what he told us a few days later. On January 20 Mr. Blue started by asking: "How does this Canadian Environmental Protection Act impinge upon those powers? Provinces too can make environmental laws and they do it under their power to legislate with respect to property and civil rights, their licensing power, and their power with respect to provincial works and undertakings. You do not have a case where one jurisdiction has the authority and the other does not". That is a very important point that he made. "You have a situation where each has jurisdiction. Each can legislate over the subject of the environment, but from a different aspect. There the legal rules are fairly clear. The rules say that unless there is an operational conflict, both laws can prevail".
Mr. Blue said: "What is an operational conflict?" Mr. Blue further stated: "Recently, I was involved in a case in the Ontario Divisional Court where we were talking about the construction of a liquid natural gas storage facility in Cobourg, Ontario. The Ontario Energy Board was hearing it and there was a National Energy Board Act and regulations. Both sets of provisions covered it. The argument was that there was an operational conflict. However, the judges said nothing conflicted. Therefore, unless the provincial law says one thing and the federal law says another so that you create an antinomy or a place where a person is in an impossible position between two valid laws, then both can stand. I believe I am correct that this is the law".
He also said: "Now if there is a conflict then the law is pretty clear too". What does it say, Mr. Speaker? "The federal legislation prevails, the provincial legislation must give way". That is the conclusion of Ian Blue.
Mr. Blue also had something interesting to say on overlapping jurisdiction. He said:
It is a well known principle that where Parliament can legislate over a topic under s.91 from one aspect, and the provinces can legislate over the same topic on another aspect that both pieces of legislation are valid. If, however, the two pieces of legislation have an operational conflict and create an antinomy then the provincial legislation is rendered inoperative and the federal legislation must prevail.
April 26, 1988

How does that now apply to Bill C-74? Mr. Blue further remarked:
If, therefore, Bill C-74 conflicts with existing provincial legislation, it is my opinion that existing provincial legislation must be inoperative to the extent of the conflict and Bill C-74 must prevail. I hasten to add that this is a legal opinion and not a political opinion ...
Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, the politicians in power, the so-called Progressive Conservative Government, did not heed this legal advice, and did not see the opportunity being offered to them by the Constitution, and by the experts. They simply put it aside and chose to go for this equivalency route, on which 1 will dwell for a little while later on.
Perhaps in a lighter vein it is interesting to note that the worries were not only on the side of the provinces, and that there were also worries on the side of the federal position. In the case of Conseil du Patronat du Quebec, the view from industry there expressed by Mr. Magnant was a search for a federal protection from the apparently very effective policies of the provincial Minister of the Environment in Quebec. This is what Mr. Magnant said to us in committee on December 16:

That protects us from the Government of Quebec.

"CELA" being the federal legislation.

We think that the federal Government is a little less strict than the Government of Quebec.
That is the opinion of Quebec businessmen.

I think it was a rather solitary viewpoint, but nevertheless it provided a touch of diversion from what most of us believe, and quite rightly so, because of the experience we have made with social and economic legislation and now emerging with environmental legislation, that really it is only the federal Government that can provide the national standards that are strong enough to protect this enormous natural resource that nature has given us, namely, the environment as a whole.
Inevitably, Mr. Speaker, I have to bring to your attention what this equivalency business is all about. It has now become a current word, at least in this legislation, and in present times in Ottawa, and it is not a concept that one can easily come to grips with. One has to wrestle with it before becoming comfortable with that concept. It is a notion we reject, but it is important to understand it. I will commence by quoting Miss Elizabeth Swanson of the Environmental Law Centre for Alberta. Last December Miss Swanson said to the committee the following:
The first matter we would like to discuss is the failure of this bill to create a strong federal presence in the area of environmental protection. Throughout the legislative history of this bill, the federal government, through its Minister
Canadian Environmental Protection Act
of Environment, promised Canadians a strong federal presence in the area of environmental protection. This came as good news to those of us who had long awaited a government response to many pressing environmental issues which appear to require a national if not a global resolution. Regrettably the provisions of this legislation as it now stands fail to achieve this objective.
The tone of this bill is apologetic rather than assertive. A conciliatory rather than a leadership approach appears to have been adopted. Consider by way of example subclause 37(4) which says that, pursuant to this provision, the Minister can only recommend regulations if, firstly, he has offered to consult with the provinces, secondly, he has consulted or the time for doing so has elapsed and, finally, he is satisfied that the provinces themselves are not going to enact similar legislation.
She goes on to say that Bill C-74 "prohibits the making of an emergency order until, among other things, the provinces have been consulted and the Minister is satisfied that appropriate provincial action is not forthcoming." She went on to say:
-the failure of the federal government to assume responsibility for the enactment and enforcement of comprehensive environmental legislation cannot be attributed to a lack of constitutional competency.
Evidently referring to Lucas and Bloom. Ms. Swanson continued:
With exclusive jurisdiction over criminal law, the federal government has always had the power to create offences and impose sanctions to enforce its own legislation. In our view, the amendments very recently put forward by the Environment Minister further erode the federal presence in this area.
The consultation approach of subclauses 37(4) and 38(2) have now been replaced by the concept of equivalency. If these amendments go forward, Cabinet will have the authority to pass an order declaring that particular and valid federal regulations do not apply in a province which has enacted and agreed to enforce equivalent provisions.
And I emphasize, Mr. Speaker, "equivalent" provisions.
This concept of equivalency surfaces again in the proposed amendments to clause 57, which concerns international air pollution. Beyond the obvious questions, such as the meaning of equivalency and the criteria by which this quality will be assessed, is a fundamental concern.
By entrenching this notion of equivalent provincial legislation, is the federal government not implicitly recognizing the competency of the provinces to legislate in an area of federal jurisdiction-
What an indictment this statement is. What far-reaching consequences this proposal, if passed, will have. Ms. Swanson continued:
-and given this recognition, what is to stop the provinces from challenging the constitutional competency of the federal government to enact legislation where the provinces' own is not recognized as being equivalent?
Just imagine what the consequences would be. She continued:
It does not appear to us either that equivalency reduces or eliminates duplication of legislative effort. To determine whether one legislation is equivalent to another, both must be in existence in one form or another. Delegation of enforcement is one thing. Abrogation of legislative competency is quite another.
There then followed some suggestions, all of which were ignored by the Government.
We also had the viewpoint of Toby Vigod, of the Environmental Law Association, who asked:

April 26, 1988
For example, does "equivalent" mean that the province also has equivalent enforcement provisions, or that the sections are very close in wording, or how close is equivalent?
That is the question. She went on to say:
1 think the other fundamental issue is the constitutional issue-that if we have a patchwork of laws where in some cases federal regulation applies and in other cases so-called provincial-equivalent regulations apply, then I have suggested federal industries charged under the provincial-equivalent regulations may bring forward an argument of Crown immunity, as they have brought forward under our existing situation.
Again, the same preoccupation we heard from the individuals from Alberta. She concluded as follows:
I think there is a danger in enacting these amendments, both for the word "equivalent" and what it may mean, and this potential constitutional problem.
On behalf of Toxic Watch Project, we heard from the Project Director, Mr. Brad Wylynko. Again, his major concern had to do with the question of "equivalency".
One might think that undue time was devoted to the question of equivalency, and that would be a justified impression were it not for the fact that the concept of "equivalency" is of paramount importance in terms of the implementation of Bill C-74, as I am sure that the Hon. Member for Red Deer will agree.
Mr. Wylynko had the following to say on the question of "equivalency":
We feel this is a very dangerous concept. I am not a constitutional lawyer, but one of the dangers we see here is that the federal government may in fact be giving up its role in environmental protection through this concept in future. If the provinces are allowed to start to legislate in replacing the federal rule, down the road will it be possible for the federal government to then come back and say they have responsibilities and obligations here they must fulfil?
I feel very strongly about this. We feel there needs to be a strong federal presence in the environment. When I look out the window of where I work, I see the North Saskatchewan River, and of course it flows from the Rocky Mountains right into Hudson Bay.
Any toxic chemical pollutant that might be in that river flows similarly, right across three prairie provinces.
I believe there needs to be a strong federal presence and, in fact, a strong international presence as well, which this bill will reduce.
Mr. Speaker, I see that we are approaching one o'clock. May I call it one o'clock?

subsubtopic: CHALLENGE'88 OPPOSITION TO BUDGETARY CUT BACKS

Mr. Speaker, over the week-end, in my riding I had the opportunity to meet several young students who expressed their great disappointment with the decision of the Tory Government to cut by nearly 40 per cent the funds earmarked for the Chal-lenge'88 program for all students living in the Greater Montreal area and the City of Laval ridings.

subsubtopic: ANNIVERSARY OF CHERNOBYL NUCLEAR REACTOR DISASTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, two years ago today, on April 26, 1986, the nuclear reactor at Chernobyl in Ukraine exploded, sending out a cloud of radiation which spread throughout the world. To this day, we do not know the full impact of the disaster.
For 48 hours the Soviet Government lowered a veil of secrecy over the tragedy even though other lives were endangered by its silence. For those with family in eastern Europe and Ukraine it was a frightening experience, as weeks passed before they were able to confirm the safety of their loved ones.
The possibility of a design flaw which might have caused the disaster has never been addressed, yet the Soviets proceed with plans to build more reactors in Ukraine. In the meantime, families who were exposed to radiation wait in fear, worrying about the long-term effects of their exposure, uncertain of their future, with no guarantee that it might not happen again.
I urge all Members of this House to join with me in commemoration of this tragic occasion, remembering those who have died, and those who must live with the uncertainty of tomorrow.
April 26, 1988

subtopic: INTERNATIONAL CO-OPERATION CANADA-SOVIET SKI EXPEDITION REACHES NORTH POLE
INTERNATIONAL CO-OPERATION CANADA-SOVIET SKI EXPEDITION REACHES NORTH POLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure that all Members of the House today would like to join me in acknowledging the great feat of the Canada-Soviet ski expedition on reaching the North Pole.
At 3.20 a.m. eastern daylight time, this group of four Canadians and nine Soviets achieved what until now was simply their dream. This is the story of ability to overcome numerous obstacles in the pursuit of a goal. The members of this expedition not only have had to deal with a cold, harsh climate, but also they have had to overcome the obstacles of different languages and different cultures.
As a Parliamentarian I am impressed with the co-operation and good will shown by these trekkers. This "Polar Bridge" expedition will help us to understand the importance of Canada-Soviet co-operation and is symbolic of the kind of international good will of which Canada can be a part.
About 40 Canadian and Soviet government representatives were planning to be at ceremonies at the North Pole. This group included superstar hockey player, Vladislav Tretiak, and our Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Masse). While flying conditions did not allow the dignitaries to witness the expedition's arrival at the North Pole, the spirit of Canada-Soviet peaceful co-operation has already been enhanced.
I, with other Members, congratulate the members of the Canadian team: Laurie Dexter, Richard Weber, Max Buxton, and Chris Holloway for their part in this historic occasion.

Mr. Speaker, Members of the House and the general public are reminded that this week is National Organ Donor Awareness Week.
The Department of National Health and Welfare is collaborating with others in special efforts to inform the public and health professionals of the benefits of transplantation and the need for donor organs and tissues.
All Canadians should take a moment to consider organ donation through which each of us can make the most generous gift, the gift of life.

Mr. Speaker, I want to deal with a problem that arises fairly frequently, regrettably, where a Government makes an overpayment to an individual under a social program.
Where the individual has had no complicity in this payment being made, it is a very unfair thing for a Government to demand repayment and to deduct sums from future payments to reclaim the amount. Individuals do not have a computer when they get a payment. They tend to assume the amount correct, and live on it.
My colleague, the Hon. Member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Baker), raised an example of veterans' payments where overpayments occur, but the situation often occurs with other social payments.
The Government should have a policy that when an overpayment is made through no complicity by the individual who receives it, the Government should not reclaim repayment for excess amounts that are paid.

subsubtopic: FLOWTHROUGH SHARES-REQUEST THAT MINISTER REVIEW HIS POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, investors have been extremely cautious, especially since the October 19 Crash. Several years ago, flow through shares were created as an investment incentive in mining exploration in Canada.
Flow through shares have been a success story in Abitibi-Temiscamingue and elsewhere in Canada and so far in the 1980's, rich gold deposits have been found in greater number than during all the past gold rushes put together.
The Crash of last October and the tax reform have severely affected the value of natural resources shares especially those involving small businesses.
Twice a year, tax shelters are selling well: at the end of the year and in May. Without these flow through shares, we could certainly not have found so many gold mines so quickly.
Mr. Speaker, we certainly have an excellent Minister of Finance in Canada, but I would suggest to him to review his position by the end of April concerning flow through shares, failing which I would have to use a more vociferous tone in May on behalf of our prospectors and my Abitibi riding.

April 26, 1988
[English]	NUCLEAR ENERGY

Mr. Speaker, as the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) prepares to go to Washington, I thought it appropriate to pass on to him words spoken more than a century ago and repeated this week by Anthony Ketchum in a letter to The Globe and Mail.
Before selling his native lands to the U.S. Government in 1854, Chief Seattle made a speech which included the following:
The air is precious to the red man for all things share the same breath-the beast, the tree, the man. The white man does not seem to notice the air he breathes. Like a man dying for many days he is numb to the stench ...
If we sell you our land you must keep it apart and sacred, as a place where even the white man can go to taste the wind that is sweetened by the meadow's flowers.
So we will consider your offer to buy our land. If we decide to accept, I will make one condition. The white man must treat the beast (and fish, birds) of this land as his brothers.
Teach your children what we have taught our children: that the earth is our mother. All things are connected like the blood which unites one family. If men spit upon the ground, they spit upon themselves. Continue to contaminate your bed and you will one night suffocate in your own waste.

Mr. Speaker, two years ago today the Chernobyl disaster occurred, although Soviet officials had said very smugly after Three Mile Island that a Three Mile Island could not happen at Chernobyl. Now Canadian officials are saying that there could not be a Chernobyl at Pickering.
If that is the case, then why is the nuclear industry so concerned about keeping nuclear liability down to $75 million, a paltry sum given the possibility of disaster? Even if there is no accident, do we not all realize that we have no safe means of disposal of either high-level of low-level radioactive wastes?
It is time that we began to look at safe renewable sources of energy. We cannot risk the future. We cannot risk the health of Canadians.
There are 50 nuclear reactors around the Great Lakes, and 24 million people depend for their drinking water on the Great Lakes. This is too much of an experiment. Let us have faith in the future by turning to safe means for energy sources, and admit that nuclear was a mistake.

subsubtopic: FRANCE'S UNDERGROUND TESTS IN SOUTH PACIFIC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, recently France shifted its underground nuclear tests from the South Pacific atoll of Mururoa to the island of Fangataufa, just 32 kilometres away. This move was made after 90 underground tests were conducted, and the island's structural integrity began to be questioned.
I believe that conducting underground nuclear testing on South Pacific islands which are mostly extinct volcanoes, is like playing Russian roulette with the environment. This region of the world has been fortunate that the atoll of Mururoa did not break up and release its deadly radiation into the ocean, creating an environmental disaster of epic proportions.
Canada must make its concerns known to France that testing in this area of the world could have severe repercussions on life.

subsubtopic: EFFECT OF FREE TRADE ON COMMERCIAL CREDIT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on April 13, I had the honour and the privilege of speaking to members of the Canadian Credit Institute on a topic of current interest that is extremely important to Canadians, and I am referring to the impact of free trade on business credit. As a result of this talk, we were able to draw certain conclusions. First of all, the free trade agreement will strengthen our economy and make us more competitive on world markets and even more confident about our own identity and our unique social and cultural environment.
Furthermore, the agreement will provide for new jobs and economic growth in the regions, both today and beyond the year 2000, and above all it will guarantee better access to our main export market.
Mr. Speaker, I sincerely believe that only people with a positive mind-set are able to meet this challenge successfully.
It is a matter of attitude, not just aptitude, and if we understand that, the rest will take care of itself.
Canadians believe in an enterprising and innovative Canada.
