Mr. Speaker, to improve road safety, the Quebec Government has declared 1988 the Quebec Year for Road Safety.
According to a recent survey, 74 per cent of Canadians buckle up. The Province of Quebec ranks first in Canada, with 85.8 per cent in 1987, compared with 67.7 per cent the year before. This is an increase of 18.1 per cent in one year.
Many road accidents are now avoided, Mr. Speaker, thanks to the new safety awareness of Canadians and Quebecers.
However, much remains to be done in this area. Many laws and regulations should be reconsidered. We could, for instance, question driving at the age of 16. Mr. Speaker, this week in my riding has been designated to celebrate the founding of La Salle General Hospital.
There will be a host of community activities to generate much needed funds that will be used to purchase specialized hospital equipment adapted to local health needs.

Bravo and many thanks to the La Salle General Hospital Fondation!

subsubtopic: BURNABY, B.C.-COLLAPSE OF ROOF ON NEW FOOD STORE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last Saturday morning in South Burnaby a near disaster occurred in which some 20 people were injured, two of them seriously. The roof of the Save-on-Foods store collapsed during the opening day ceremonies to which senior citizens from the community were invited.
I am deeply concerned that a number of important questions be answered with respect to this tragedy. There must be a full public inquiry to determine, for example, whether in the rush to complete this project safety standards were not fully met. There must be a full inquiry to determine whether the fact that non-union labour was used in the latter stages of construction was an element in this tragedy.

April 26, 1988

subsubtopic: ACID RAIN-PRIME MINISTER'S MEETING WITH UNITED STATES PRESIDENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Prime Minister I have a question for the Secretary of State for External Affairs. On Friday in the House the Minister asserted the Government's commitment to obtaining an accord with the United States on acid rain that would commit both Governments to specific levels of reductions in emissions. Regrettably, earlier in the week the Minister of the Environment publicly said, and I use his words, that the Government had no expectation of any progress at the summit.
Then, on the weekend, in interviews with a number of American journalists, the Prime Minister seemed to pin all his hopes on the potential successors to President Reagan. Once again he was implying that nothing could be expected from the summit.
My question to the Minister is simply this. If the Government is serious about obtaining some commitment in the meetings in Washington that are coming up, why in heaven's name is the Minister saying he does not expect anything? Why is the Prime Minister sending a message to the President in advance that he does not expect anything? Is that any way to negotiate?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: ACID RAIN-PRIME MINISTER'S MEETING WITH UNITED STATES PRESIDENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that may occur because we are under an obligation, which we respect, to answer questions in the House of Commons and elsewhere. We try to do that as frankly and forthrightly as we can.
We very much hope that we can make progress on acid rain at the summit and in other meetings. However, we do not expect that we are going to have the kind of progress that we seek. Consequently, we are continuing to seek progress across the range of the American system on the acid rain question
which is so crucial to us. I think that position, which is consistent and effective, has been understood by the Americans, and is understood by most Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, it certainly does not say much for the special relationship that is supposed to have existed between the President and our Prime Minister for four years.
Since the Minister is evidently sincere about his commitment to obtaining such an accord, and since he is being frank with the House about his low expectations from the President, in non-inflammatory language why does the Government of Canada not say that as a bottom line what we will take as a minimum at this summit-after considering all the information on the seriousness of acid rain available to both countries-is that President Reagan should commit himself to specific levels of reductions in emissions? Why do we not say that in advance?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that position has been made clear by the Government of Canada in a draft treaty or agreement that we prepared. It was prepared by Canada as a consequence of the undertaking that was given here on the floor of the House of Commons by President Reagan.
As was the case when I answered a very similar question on Friday in the House, I do not have the precise text of his speech here, but my recollection is quite clear that he then said that he was prepared to consider the Prime Minister's proposal for an accord. We followed that up and made some recommendations that included reference to specific targets.
That is the Canadian position, as, by the way, and the Hon. Member will recall this, it was the position of a preceding Canadian Government with respect to the Great Lakes Water Agreement on which the Americans wanted, at that time, to avoid establishing specific targets, and the Government of the day in 1972, to its credit, insisted on that type of standard and target. We are following the same type of approach with respect to acid rain.

speechtext:

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Government Orders. Ms. Copps: 1 rise on a point of order, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Government Orders.
The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. McMillan that Bill C-74, an Act respecting the protection of the environment and of human life and health, be read the third time and passed.

Mr. Speaker, just before the one o'clock break, you were patiently listening to an elaboration of Bill C-74, and I was taking you through the question of equivalency. At that time, I was drawing to your attention a statement made by Brad Wylynko of the Toxic Watch project when he tackled the matter of equivalency last December in committee. On this important development, the introduction of the concept of equivalency in a piece of federal legislation, he said the following:
-the term "equivalency" Is very ambiguous and vague. It is very difficult to pin down just what that term means. It is obviously not identical, or it should say that. I ask myself whether it could be equal in effect or equal in purpose.
If that is the case, then I might give you a scenario. Let us say the Province of Alberta decides that under its Provincial Transport of Dangerous Goods Legislation, its regulations of PCB transportation within the province are equivalent-as equal in effect or equal in purpose-to the federal regulations. If it is argued as such, and Cabinet sees it as such, then the provincial legislation will be the one that is used.
To what extent is it necessarily equal? Is it necessarily equal in all the standards, the standards of construction of the vehicles that are transporting the PCBs, the emergency equipment? To what level does this equality extend? To what degree of specificity does it extend?

April 26, 1988
Canadian Environmental Protection Act
Mr. Wylynko raises very important, fundamental questions. The third problem he raises with the term "equivalency" is the question of who then does the monitoring, assessment and enforcement under these equivalent provisions. That is a very important question.
One would assume, he argues, that if it is provincial legislation being used instead of federal legislation, then it would be provincial monitoring, enforcement and prosecution that would be used if there were a contravention of that legislation or regulation. Through this equivalency provision, the federal Government may be giving up the whole whereas under the federal legislation, there might be $1 million fines available for a breach of the legislation or regulation. Under the provincial legislation, again using the example of Alberta, it would be $25,000. You may be going against the entire intent of the Act by allowing the provincial legislation to be the legislation used in that case.
This morning I brought to your attention Dr. Alistair Lucas' statement on equivalency. He must be again brought back into this debate because he made the following statement to us on January 26:
If some provincial legislation is accepted as equivalent under these provisions but other provincial legislation is not so that Bill C-74 applies in those provinces, you then have a patchwork of federal and provincial environmental protection legislation.
That is what it will boil down to. If you want to hear an eminently responsible statement on this complex question then I urge you to listen to that made by Friends of the Earth who, in their brief to the committee, and it is just one paragraph but it says it all very well, said this:
Granted the government may wish to arrange for a province to carry out federal requirements and will appropriately consult with the relevant provincial Governments. However, the ultimate authority should flow from and rest with the federal government. As it stands, the amendments force the Minister to take an "after you" approach to environmental protection and effectively strip the Government of authority.
They recommend that the original section which required mandatory consultation with the provinces and the amendments which provide for exemption of the provinces from application of federal legislation be deleted. Unfortunately, that advice went by unheeded.
It is interesting again to note, as I brought to your attention this morning, the observation by Conseil du patronat du Quebec:

. .. le Conseil du patronat du Quebec, when it told the Committee: Finally, the federal-provincial agreements required for the implementation of this bill are not clearly defined. What standards will prevail? Federal or povincial? Will we have a homogeneous system all across Canada, or will there be important regional variants? A lot of questions have yet to be answered, in our opinion, in that respect,

These questions are still to be clarified.
Enough on equivalency. I have now to take you to the question of the Bill of Rights and a concept that is a good idea per se, that was in a way touched upon on a number of occasions by the Minister, but which has been left now without teeth, without muscle, unfortunately. It was very well put to us
by Paul Muldoon of Energy Probe when in committee he made the following points:
What is needed is a straightforward, unequivocal declaration. We can say ... that all people of Canada have a statutory right to a healthy environment, a right that can be enforced in the courts. Consequently, it would establish the government as a trustee of all public lands, waters, and resources of the province, and impose obligations on it to conserve and maintain the resources. It really identifies and clarifies that each person in Canada has a right to a healthy environment.
There are some clauses within this proposed bill which deal with what I would call an environmental bill of rights. As a lawyer, I am afraid they do not help me very much.
He then elaborated on a couple of cases and continued:
There are also other clauses which, if you wish, I can deal with, but that is the main thrust. An environment bill of rights therefore is accountability. It is accountability for everyone, individuals, industry and government, and it allows those people who need protection or those who want to enforce the act the opportunity to do so.
Right this minute, before the Ontario Legislature, second reading is being debated on a bill called An Environmental Bill of Rights for Ontario, a copy of which I have included in the package of material. I urge this committee to recommend certain reforms that parallel that... that bill does propose to give each person in Ontario an environmental bill of rights, which will be essentially the right to a healthy environment and the right to enforce that right.
On the same occasion he went on to say:
The way to do it, though, is that clause 128 would simply say anyone, not just those who have suffered a loss or damage, can seek relief in a court of competent jurisdiction who suspects another person, industry or government is breaching a standard of a provision of the act, period.
The first thing would be to remove, and this is a very important passage in the Bill before us, the words "who has suffered loss or damage". The suggestion was made that it should instead read "any person may go to a court of competent jurisdiction to sue and recover". In other words, the provision "who has suffered loss or damage" is a barrier to action by the individual citizen to protect the environment. If you represent a non-government organization, an environmental group, you cannot go to court to enforce the Act. You have to find someone who suffered damage from a breach of that Act. That is what it boils down to with respect to who has the right to take action to protect the environment.
The problem, he went on to say, is virtually that it is impossible in environmental litigation to connect the damage to the source, the damage to the act. A classic case is the Toronto lead smelters. For years a number of industries have been polluting the city with lead to the detriment of children and environmental health at large. However, to prove lead emissions from a company caused those precise injuries to those children is virtually impossible because lead comes from all types of sources, including automobiles. The molecule of lead that damaged the lungs and metabolism of a child, did it come from a certain industry? It is a standard which is impossible to prove and which would render Clause 128 of this Bill totally inoperative.
Therefore, Mr. Muldoon concluded that under this clause he could not proceed because he has not suffered injury or damage. Only a pollution victim, probably for many of the toxic chemicals, can do so. The latency period is anywhere from five to 20 years in some types of contamination. Lead contamination in Toronto is a perfect example. Why does one
April 26, 1988

want to wait until harm occurs, he asks? His recommendation was to remove the standing barrier. Let anyone enforce the law. What is everyone hiding? If someone is breaking the law, certainly they should be put in a position where they have to comply with the law.
This is not a revolutionary program. It is a simple, logical program where one says that here is an environmental group which is environmentally sensitive and active. It sees industry, an individual or a Government contravening the law. Why can they not go to court and enforce the law? It can be done in common law, Mr. Muldoon concluded.
It is interesting to note that the Minister himself, when he appeared before the committee on November 25 last year said:
I am more concerned, frankly, about lack of accountability. 1 think it is terribly important that some of the enforcement clout of a bill involve the citizen, the individual who is affected, when a given chemical violates the environment and perhaps human health.
I applaud the Minister for having said that. The only problem is that it is not in the Bill. Having preached the substance and the theory, the will is not in the Bill. That is what led me to say earlier that this legislation has a history of retreats, contradictions, and flip-flops. That is one example of that.
It is also important to put on the record what the Canadian Environmental Law Association in Toronto said through Toby Vigod in January of this year.
CELA since its inception in 1970, has been advocating the need for such a bill of rights at both the federal and provincial levels of government. It would seem essential that any comprehensive revision of federal environmental law be updated in its provision of public rights to protect the environment. "Key provisions would include the right to a healthy environment and the right of a member of the public to seek a declaration or injunction for actual or threatened environmental harm,-
Again reference is made to Clause 128 which, Ms. Vigod concluded, can in no way be called an environmental bill of rights and should be amended to provide for broader rights for citizens to protect their environment.
In an editorial in The Intervenor, the newsletter of the Canadian Environmental Law Association, in November, 1986, Toby Vigod wrote:
The EPA does not contain, or even come close to being, an Environmental Bill of Rights, even though the Minister has claimed it to be. While there is a lengthy preamble stressing the importance of environmental protection, preambles are not legally enforceable, and would only be used as an aid for interpreting otherwise ambiguous sections of the Act.
A real Environmental Bill of Rights would contain some of the following elements:
-the right of the Canadian public to a healthful, aesthetically and culturally viable environment; recognition of a public trust in Canada's lands, water and resources; the right of any member of the public to bring a lawsuit for actual or threatened environmental harm or breach of a federal law.
Canadian Environmental Protection Act
without the necessity of having to show personal injury or property interests of that individual; the right of the public to become involved in the federal environmental decision-making process, such rights to include input into the standard setting process and the right to financial assistance, where necessary, to ensure effective public participation.
In 1979 in a debate in this Chamber the present Minister of the Environment eloquently supported the need for an environmental bill of rights. The Bill at that time would have incorporated many of the proposals advanced by the Canadian Environmental Association in this editorial which concludes:
Unfortunately, these sentiments have not been transferred to the proposed EPA.
Another important chapter in the discussion of this Bill at third reading has to do with federal polluters. I must pay tribute to the Member for York East (Mr. Redway) for the fine role he played in committee, alas, without achieving the intent which he had in mind. However, he certainly put very forcefully a position which we in the Opposition shared and would have very much liked to have seen adopted as an amendment in the Bill itself. The issue was put quite lucidly by Pollution Probe through Kai Millyard on January 20 of this year when he appeared before the committee. He said:
Probably the most important is in Part IV of the bill-federal lands, works, undertakings and all of that. This concern really only crystalized for us about a week ago when we learned that a number of federal government agencies- Transport Canada and the National Research Council-over the last few years had been releasing some of the hazardous wastes they generate in the process of doing what they do, to an unlicensed trucking company that discharged those wastes into a sewer grate here in Ottawa going out to the Ottawa River.
I would like to pay a special compliment to my colleague, the Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) who has, on a number of occasions by himself in this House, raised the question of pollution by federal government agencies.
Mr. Millyard went on to say:
The provincial government, which does have standards and regulations about these matters, charged those agencies with violations of the Ontario Environmental Protection Act.
In court the Department of Justice argued federal immunity to provincial laws. Unfortunately, the judge agreed with that argument and the charges were quashed, although I gather the province is now preparing an appeal. This kind of federal immunity might not be such a problem except for the fact that Environment Canada does not regulate the polluters for which the federal government is responsible.
If it did, if there were regulations that applied to all of those companies-we mean corporations that are federally incorporated, such as banks, airlines, railways, shipping concerns and so on, as well as any activities that take place in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon. Of course, provincial laws do not apply there and Environment Canada is the only possible environmental regulator ... However, the simple message is that Crown immunity really is a concept that is not popular with the public. Pollution Probe certainly sees absolutely no reason why the federal government should not have to meet environmental laws.

April 26, 1988
Canadian Environmental Protection Act
Neither does the public, Mr. Speaker, and neither do, I am sure, the vast majority of Members in this House.
Mr. Millyard concluded as follows:
Whether they are the provincial laws in which the federal agencies operate or whether it is a new licensing regime set up by the federal government is less important. In our view the federal government must control its own polluters if it expects to have any credibility at all.
These are pretty clear and convincing words and they were backed up by the Canadian Environmental Law Association by Toby Vigod. On the preceding day in committee she said:
We are concerned about the federal Government's failure to exercise its clear authority to regulate federal works and undertakings under exclusive federal jurisdiction.
It is clear as a bell. She then elaborated on the 1981 prosecution by the Ontario Ministry of the Environment of Eldorado Nuclear for a spill into Lake Ontario. She said:
In that case, charges brought under the Ontario Water Resources Act were thrown out of court on the basis that Eldorado, as a federal Crown corporation, was immune from the application of provincial law, as the legislation did not expressly, or by implication, bind the Crown. More recently the National Research Council and council employees were charged under the Ontario Environmental Protection Act with illegal transfers of waste to an unauthorized waste hauler without completion of any waste manifests as required by the regulations. Again, the Provincial Court held that the Ontario legislation did not bind the federal Crown and the charges were dismissed. The unfortunate result is that federal agencies can continue to hide behind Crown immunity and act in an environmentally unsound manner.
Here we had a golden opportunity, because we cannot amend the legislation every second year and we cannot go frequently into an important exercise such as Bill C-74. We had a terrific opportunity to rectify what is definitely a scandal in the operation on the part of some federal Departments and agencies. That opportunity was missed, and I will explain in a moment why.
The spokesperson for the Environmental Law Centre in Edmonton, Linda Duncan, spoke on December 10 with respect to federal works and undertakings, and this is the explanation as to why the golden opportunity was missed:
... the Bill requires the concurrence of the federal Minister responsible for administering that particular work or undertaking or land before the Minister of the Environment may bring forward regulations for the protection of the environment.
Will the Minister of Transport of the day agree with the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) to correct the situation, or with the Minister in charge of Science and Technology as it affects the NRC? We know what the obvious answer is.
Miss Duncan went on to say:
Again, it is our assertion that this provision runs contrary to the stated political intent that the Canadian Environmental Protection Act be viewed as the vehicle to centralize and consolidate protection of the environment. To require the assent of the Ministry proposed to be regulated is to diminish the effect of Part IV of the Bill.
I think she used very mild words when she said "diminish". She said a political decision must be made, and quite rightly
so, whether to empower the Minister of the Environment to act to protect the environment. She went on to say:
A wise Minister will consult with the affected Ministry regardless of legislative requirements. The affected Ministry is also accorded the opportunity of raising objections at the cabinet level.
Many of us in committee fought to have at least this approach taken, but we did not succeed. It is interesting to hear what John McCallum of Ecology North had to say on January 19. He said:
In the North we paid a lot of attention to Part IV of the Bill, which deals with federal lands and waters. We have long felt that the northern environment is particularly poorly regulated and that we need a more comprehensive system with less discretionary power and greater public input to decisions. Environment Canada also has an environmental role in the North through its responsibility to administer Section 33 of the Fisheries Act. However, the overlap between this section and the Northern Inland Waters Act has never been cleared up.
The GNWT also has some environmental legislation. Although its constitutional basis is cloudy. It does have a clear mandate for management of forestry and wildlife which the Department of Indian and Northern Development has transferred to it.
The federal Government, with DIAND in the lead role, has continued to allow the situation to exist for years with no effort to clarify constitutional responsibility, fill legislative gaps or urge the to do so. For those of us who are environmentally conscious this has not only been frustrating, we feel it is negligence. So it was with great hope that we saw what was originally Part III of CEPA as the portent of someone who was prepared to take responsibility for setting up and enforcing comprehensive, systematic, strict environmental legislation in the NWT.
But a more careful analysis showed that Environment Canada was still nervous about stepping on toes in other jurisdictions-just as, in the original section of CEPA,
DOE worded the Bill so they could only act in consultation with the Minister responsible and only to enact regulations in areas where no other legislation existed or to set guidelines for departments.
So it seems that the Department of the Environment is continuing in the tradition of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development of avoiding the issue. He concluded by saying: "Mr. McMillan's words seem hollow".
Let me move on now to national standards, which is a very important subject as well. It is interesting to note that on November 25, 1987, when we were graced by the Minister's presence in committee, he said:
We are setting in place a Canada-wide regime for the management of certain forms of pollution, in this context, chemicals; it is a cradle-to-grave approach to management of toxic chemicals. We want to set a national standard below which no province would plunge.
You should read, Mr. Speaker, in the record the acrobatic elaborations through which the Minister's own Parliamentary Secretary went last week in order to avoid using the words national standards and replacement with national control standards, which means quite a different thing. The Minister said: "This does not mean that an individual province like Ontario, which might well have regulations specific to circumstances that are above our national standards, would be prevented from enforcing them". He set the foundation, the framework, for what some of us thought was going to be a pretty good and solid elaboration of the discussion leading to the setting of national standards.
April 26, 1988

I welcome the arrival of the Parliamentary Secretary to join in this debate because it is very important to her, considering the discussion we had last week at the report stage of this Bill.
When discussing the subject, it would take hours and hours to relay everything that was said on the question of standards, but it is worthwhile for a moment to report what was said by Richard Martin, the spokesperson for the Canadian Labour Congress when he took a crack at the subject of standards. He said:
On a philosophical basis I suppose we basically agree with a strong central Government establishing uniform controls across the country, because partially what they say is correct. The competition of allowing one polluter, if I can so speak, to have a larger area or more leeway to pollute than another jurisdiction may work against a province's interest to attract investment and development in the province, if it wants to have a clean environment, compared with another province that is lax on its particular laws.
Through various bodies, we have recommended national standards in terms of occupational health and safety matters and limits in terms of exposure to chemicals.
We have also recommended the same thing in terms of the environment. On the other hand, it is quite important to us that national recommended standards should be in place before provinces are allowed to give up or abrogate their responsibilities in terms of the environment, clean air, or any other matter. Otherwise, we are going to have a whole open period during which pretty well anybody can do anything to the environment.
That is the fear that Mr. Martin brought out in committee. He concluded by saying:
I would recommend that we try to establish those recommended national standards for introduction into the provinces, keeping in mind that the provinces do have many rights and should exercise those rights in terms of cleaning up the environment.
This was a pretty reasonable approach I thought. In a way it was reinforced by Barbara McElgunn when she appeared before the committee on January 19 and stated:
We know that Canadians deserve health and environmental protection via national standards for air and water quality. However, it appears that the federal government does not have this authority-
She is quite right. The Parliamentary Secretary confirmed it in the debate last week. We will go into that since I have studied the terminology that she used. I will prove to you, Mr. Speaker, that this notion has been abandoned, as well as why and how.
If the Parliamentary Secretary disagrees with me then she does not understand what she is saying in the House, which is even more serious.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext: You are misinterpreting the witnesses.

The Minister is expected to formulate guidelines and objectives with respect to the environment under this Bill. It is then doubtful, said Mrs. McElgunn, that there will be a federal authority to establish maximum intolerable concentrations for contaminants in air and drinking water in Canada for Canadians. She said that it is doubtful. She went on to say that it is noteworthy that the Decima report in December, 1987, placed drinking water quality at the top of Canadian environmental concerns. She concluded by saying
Canadian Environmental Protection Act
that standards have the force of regulations whereas guidelines and objectives do not.
We have said enough about that subject, except that, when he appeared before the committee on the same day, Mr. Millyard of Pollution Probe made these two very important and clear points. I quote:
In the 1970s, both under the Clean Air Act and under the Fisheries Act, there were programs the government had, which were systematically going through the industrial sectors that were thought or known to be major sources of pollution, and, along with those industries, were writing regulations and standards to gradually limit and clean up the emissions of those industries. Those programs are gone, both in the Fisheries Act and in the Clean Air Act.
This is another item about which we had lengthy discussions in committee to no avail. Mr. Millyard concluded by saying that there were standards written for four categories of industries under the Clean Air Act. He said that those are being rolled over into this law, and the ability actually to launch programs like that and write such standards is still in Bill C-74, but he is very concerned that there is no program to do these things. That is separate from the statute itself.
As I said, the question of national standards is one that one cannot stress forcefully enough and long enough. However, we have to move on. I could take Hon. Members through the whole question of enforcement of this legislation. It is important that we understand what the Government is offering Canadians here in the words of the Government and those who study the operations of Government. It is important to quote two paragraphs from a study prepared by the Canadian Environmental Advisory Council which reports to the Minister himself. I am quoting from its study of January, 1987 which states:
Our review of the EPS delegation scheme suggests that federal delegation of environmental enforcement authority amounts to a virtual abdication of responsibility for enforcement and has promoted discrepancies in the nature of enforcement responses across Canada ... Council is of the opinion that some current trends, such as the delegation of administrative powers to provincial authorities and excessive fears of federal-provincial conflicts, are having negative effects on the implementation of Environment Canada's legislative mandate, and undermine the confidence of Canadians in the Department.
This was not written by some fly-by-night operator, or by a critic of the environment. This was written by the Canadian Environmental Advisory Council under the title: "Enforcement Practices of Environment in Canada". This is a very serious observation that is made which has an important bearing on what will be the effect of this Bill, which in the way it is worded now negates the very spirit and substance of the observation made by the very Council which advises the Minister. So much for consultation and so much for listening to advice.
On the question of enforcement it is also important to have on record an observation made by Ross Hume Hall to which my distinguished colleague from Red Deer referred in his speech this morning. In an essay published in the spring of last year he wrote:

April 26, 1988
Adjournment Debate
The single-chemical approach breaks down under the sheer weight of the
60,000 existing industrial chemicals. To illustrate the absurdity of trying to
regulate industrial chemicals in this manner, let us do a simple calculation.
The 19 member bureaucratic team of the Contaminants Control Branch took
10 years to assess-
Guess how many, Mr. Speaker? Five chemicals. It took 10 years to assess five chemicals, that is, 190 bureaucrat-years to write five regulations, 38 bureaucrat years per chemical. Imagine that Environment Canada puts all its 10,000 employee-years from janitor to Deputy Minister, if you like, all of them, to this task. Actually, now, because of the transfer of the Canadian Forestry Service to Agriculture Canada and because of the cuts in November, 1984, and losses to inflation and the like, to an amount of well over $60 million in its purchasing power, its establishment of strength is now less than 7,000 individuals, I believe. Suppose that Environment Canada puts all its employees to work-the assumption here is 10,000, which is 50 per cent greater than today-to write the regulations. At that rate the Department could write 260 per year. The Department would not keep up with 1,000 new chemicals that enter commerce every year.
If this calculation is correct, and it comes from a person who has a very high standing, so much so that he was appointed to head this special group to which the Hon. Member referred this morning in his speech, to answer this type of emerging problem here as defined by Ross Hume Hall, what does the Government do to make funds available for enforcement? Over the next five years it makes available $37 million to be divided among three Departments. If my arithmetic is correct, $7.4 million a year, divided by three, is approximately $2.5 million per Department to enforce this type of monstrosity. Therefore, one has to conclude that the enforcement aspect, which there is no doubt is a very massive and difficult one, is not being given the administrative, bureaucratic muscle needed to carry out such a massive task, particularly in consideration of the point made by Ross Hume Hall that at the present time there are some 1,000 new chemicals that enter commerce every year.
What is omitted in this Bill is an important aspect that I will touch upon briefly. It deals with our native people and it deals with an international river. I am referring to the question of international riparian rights. I realize that this is a complex issue, but nevertheless it has to be put on the record. I am referring to the brief prepared by the Citizens' Coalition for Clean Water. It was sent to all Members of Parliament in Canada and to the media. It bears the date of April 14, 1988, so it is very recent. In four lines it sets out the problem very well by first quoting Mark Twain. I am sure that the Hon. Member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers) with a penchant for poetry will enjoy this. Mark Twain said, "The Mississippi is a very muddy river, too thick to drink, and too thin to plough".
The Coalition for Clean Water went on to say, "Mr. Twain could clearly see the state of his river, but people in Wal-laceburg, Ontario and Walpole Island Indian Reserve cannot".
In a very eloquent, touching, and short manner, the Citizens' Coalition for Clean Water describes to each one of us the situation along that river caused by upstream pollution. It places high hopes in the Canadian Environmental Protection Act, and it urges us to take certain action. It states, "You can reinstate the original preamble of January, 1986", and this is why earlier in my remarks I made a reference to this Bill as being a history of retreat and flip-flops. The Coalition urges us collectively that, "You can reinstate the original preamble of January, 1986, whose language was closely akin to extending environmental rights to all Canadians". This is where the recognition was in the original draft. I cannot understand for the life of me why we gave it up, because it was good stuff. It deserved to remain untouched. This is a point made by Don Laprise, the Chairman, and John Wilkinson, the Secretary-Treasurer in this brief. They go on to state:
You can reword Section 100 so that ordinary Canadians can gain, unhindered, full access to the law, and stand in court on an equal, legal and financial footing with corporate polluters.
I now ask you, Mr. Speaker, who would disagree with that stuff? I do not see anyone who would disagree with that type of approach. It makes eminent sense. I am sure that even members of the Progressive Conservative Party while campaigning in the next election might take a stand like this in their own ridings. They will sense the pressure of the public to take that type of stance and translate it into legislation.
The Coalition concluded by stating:
The Parliament of Canada has a trust responsibility to provide all Canadians with a pollution free environment. We strongly urge you as a lawmaker to bring the Canadian Environmental Protection out of the sky and down to the level of the ordinary person where it can be environmentally useful, where it can preserve, protect and eventually be celebrated.
These are beautiful words, Mr. Speaker, of substance and poetry. For the life of me, I cannot understand why collectively we were not able to master sufficient will to do exactly that. That is enough said, Mr. Speaker, on the subject of riparian rights, because time is going by.
