April 26, 1988
The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. McMillan that Bill C-74, an Act respecting the protection of the environment and of human life and health, be read the third time and passed.

I welcome your interruption, Mr. Speaker, and I will now move on to the subject of the discussion that took place here last week when, by way of our procedure, we debated a number of motions at the so-called report stage. We began with a ruling from the Speaker who gave us an indication of how to proceed.
It so happened that the motion in my name that came up for debate early that day dealt with the desirability to introduce in Clause 2, which is the preamble, a paragraph to the effect that the intent of this measure is to endeavour to establish national standards of environmental quality. Why did we do that, Mr. Speaker? Because the Bill as it is presently worded is weak and it does not reflect and contain the political will with which the same Bill was announced by the Minister himself. It has lost steam, it has lost fire, and it has lost muscle. With that motion, by at least putting an intent in the preamble, I was endeavouring to bring back some of that.
The Government did announce that the Bill was a great measure to clean up the environment, which it does not, unfortunately; and that it would open up a new era for the protection of the environment from damage, for which it does not provide the necessary funds in the enforcement of it.
It was interesting to note that in the draft Bill entitled "Proposed Environmental Protection Act", which goes back to 1986, on page 1 there was a subparagraph which stated: "Provide leadership in the establishment of nationally consistent standards of environmental quality". Would you believe, Mr. Speaker, it was there. It is now gone. We proposed it and we lost. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, why that retreat? That particular measure in the draft Bill, which was the object of consultations, received widespread public support across the country through those public consultations. It became almost a challenge to attempt to bring it back by way of a motion at the report stage. What we have in its stead is the phrase "endeavour to establish nationally consistent levels of environmental quality".
We have moved from providing leadership in the establishment of nationally consistent "standards" of environmental quality to endeavouring to establish nationally consistent "levels" of environmental quality. One is quite a far cry from the other.
Canadian Environmental Protection Act
In the Bill as it is currently drafted, the emphasis is on consistency. The Government went through an extensive public consultation process in respect of this legislation, and I imagine it did so with the best of intentions. In doing so, however, it created the impression that there was a genuine attempt to consult with the public, and having done so it then retreated from the strong wording of the Bill as introduced to "nationally consistent levels of environmental quality".
There is a world of difference between "levels" and "standards". What a shame!
When a Government retreats from the political will of wanting to establish "national standards" into the mushy world of endeavouring to establish "nationally consistent levels", one has to ask oneself what has happened to the political will of that Government.
What has caused the Government to make a 180 degree turn, backtracking from the strong language of the Bill as first introduced? No longer do we have "national standards"; rather, we have consistency.
I look forward to hearing the response of the Parliamentary Secretary, or perhaps that of the Minister himself on this particular point. An explanation ought to be put on the record, and I invite the Minister or his Parliamentary Secretary to put something of substance on the record in this respect.
The Parliamentary Secretary, in her reply, said that what I was proposing was a seemingly minor amendment to the "administrative duties" section of the Bill. She went on to say that the consequence of this seemingly innocent word change would be to impair the very goal that I was seeking, and she thereafter engaged in a number of points, all of which, to me, are simply sophistry of a kind that is the reflection of a muddled mind. Having reread the record of that debate, that is all I can say. To give you but one example, the Parliamentary Secretary went on to make the point that the word "levels" allows for a "range of regulatory possibilities, guidelines for industries to follow, objectives to be aimed at, codes of practice to be adhered to, standards to be achieved, and outright bans to be implemented, if required".
Mr. Speaker, the Parliamentary Secretary is dreaming in Technicolor, to say the least. The fact that the existence of standards is important is demonstrated and reinforced through our experience with acid rain, in respect of which standards were established, with the abatement programs then following. Given the Canadian geology and climatology, we set a standard in respect of the deposition of wet sulphides, the standard being that the deposition of wet sulphides should not exceed 50 kilograms per hectare per year. That was a scientifically arrived at standard, and from that standard we then developed our policies.

April 26, 1988
Canadian Environmental Protection Act
That standard proved to be good for Canada, and it is one that has served us well since its implementation. Given that experience, I felt that there was sufficient ground to ensure the entrenching of the word "standards" in the legislation.
I am tempted to read to you some of the evidence in respect of Clause 8, namely that of Pollution Probe and Friends of the Earth; but to do so would be to infringe upon the territory of the Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald), and so I shall refrain from doing so. It was very good evidence, and I trust that the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood will find the time to highlight some of it during the course of this debate.
During the report stage, there was some discussion in respect of the representation of industry, labour and nongovernmental groups. We wanted to entrench that concept in the law. We wanted to ensure that the sectorial reality of Canada will be entrenched in the legislation. Having involved labour in the deliberations on the draft Bill in committee, we felt it only natural that the description of the advisory committee be such that the various sectors will be specifically spelled out, namely, industry, labour and non-governmental groups, or public interest groups.
Unfortunately, we did not succeed in that endeavour. And why did we not succeed? Here again we heard an interesting reply from the Parliamentary Secretary, who said that there is already an advisory board, the Canadian Environmental Advisory Council, which advises the Minister, and that that should do.
In my view, this piece of legislation requires an advisory board of its own. It is unfortunate that that particular proposal was not accepted. In my view, it is one that had some merit.
We then moved on to a motion that endeavoured to delete the mandatory consultation between the federal Minister of the Environment and a committee which would be essentially federal-provincial in nature, and we did so for the reasons already outlined. In our view, such mandatory consultation would only slow down the process-an undesirable result, given that, in most instances, protection of the environment requires swift action. We also attempted to delete the equivalency policy. Finally, we attempted to remove the requirement that another federal Minister, other than the Minister of the Environment, would have to give concurrence or the green light when the Environment Minister of the day wants to proceed and lay charges against a specific Department or an agency of the Crown.
We did not go very far with these suggestions. We had to accept the will of the Minister through the Parliamentary Secretary and of the Government as a whole. That is where the
blame rests, Mr. Speaker, in having back-peddled and retreated furiously under pressure from some quarters, which I am not in a position to name but which I can guess.
We then come to the question of the national standards again. I made reference to it when the Parliamentary Secretary was here a short while ago. Here we have an intervention on behalf of the Government, and I quote the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment (Mrs. Browes) who said, as reported at page 14658 of Hansard for April 20:
-this Bill does provide for national standards-
She has news for us. The Bill provides for national standards. Then she quickly added:
-national environmental control standards, and I emphasize the adjective
"control".
That is where the nice twist comes in. She went on to say:
These control standards provided for in Sections 33 and 53 will apply-
The notion of control standards is one that must be examined for a moment in debate on third reading. We have to understand what the Parliamentary Secretary means. If environmental protection is equivalent to emission controls, emission controls must be equalized to so much per polluter. That, in turn, must probably mean that each new polluter is permitted to add to pollution. In that sense the total pollution in the end increases. In other words, the controls that have been envisaged and transmitted to us by the Parliamentary Secretary are controls that apply to the totality of the environment, no matter how many polluters there will be between now and 50 years from now.
It is, in other words, not as I said before, the establishment of standards that are permissible as a total load of pollution that indicates the tolerance of the particular environment to a specific load produced by a certain emission, by a certain industry. Having established the tolerance, you work your way back and say that there shall not be more pollution than that which the environment can tolerate. If today there are 10 polluters, so much will be the total tolerance that the environment can take from those 10 polluters. If tomorrow there will be 15 and 10 years from now 25 and so on, that tolerance remains the same. Therefore, the pollution allowed to each individual polluter will have to be decreased accordingly.
This is not what the Bill says. The Bill says that there will be a control that will be applied to each polluter and if the polluters increase in numbers, the amount of total pollution will also increase accordingly and the environment will go to hell in the process. That is what the words control standards in essence mean. That is why national standards per se in the Bill were not accepted by the Government. We are taking the wrong tack with this Bill in its very essence as to what it endeavours to do.
April 26, 1988

The Bill endeavours to establish controls on what the emitters will be allowed to pollute, but it does not establish what the environment can tolerate, and having done that, work its way back to establish how much each polluter, be it five industries today and 59 twenty-five years from now, can pollute. This is from where the serious flaw and damage will arise.
We had enough exchanges on that. It is not an easy part of the Bill to deal with, I must admit, even at third reading without time limitation. But I felt this had to be put on the record.
I will move on now to the question of the cost of investigation from a polluter. In committee, we had in the Bill, almost until the last moment a clause which said that in certain circumstances the Minister may collect the cost of investigation from a polluter. There may be circumstances when the Crown may want to recover the cost from investigating a situation caused by a polluter.
That situation could arise. The clause was right there in the Bill. One day toward the conclusion of the debate we had a motion by the Hon. Member for Niagara Falls (Mr. Nicholson) which said that that clause should be removed. It read that "where an offender has been convicted of an offence under this Act, in addition to any other punishment that may be imposed under this Act, the court may, having regard to the nature of the offence and the circumstances surrounding its commission, make an order having any or all of the following effects"-and this is the item in question-"(g) direct the offender to compensate the Minister in whole or in part for the cost of any remedial or preventive action taken by or caused to be taken on behalf of the Minister as a result of the Act or emission that constituted the offence".
That was in the Bill almost until the last minute. In his greater wisdom, the Member from Niagara Falls, supported by the majority of the government Members, managed to pull it out. What were the reasons given, Mr. Speaker? If I remember correctly, the reason was that it was unprecedented. It is that mind-set which cannot understand that progress has to set a precedent. You cannot be a member of the Progressive Conservative Party and impede progress at the same time. You cannot say that you have to delete a clause in a Bill because it is unprecedented. "It cannot be there because it has never been done before". That is a contradiction in turn to anyone who, bless his heart, joins the Progressive Conservative Party. It is inconsistent, yet here it happened.
I am trying to find the passage in committee when the Member for Niagara Falls made the point, because it is a jewel. He said, "I do not know who the opposition is that you are referring to, but I will explain why I put this in"-which is the motion-"This Bill provides for fines and imprisonment and it allows the court to charge someone who has been found guilty with the cost of remedial action." He went on to say: "I think that is fair and I am certainly not making excuses for polluters or anyone else, but I would take the same stand if this
Canadian Environmental Protection Act
was a Criminal Code offence. Mr. Caccia says it is unprecedented within the Criminal Code which it is". Here we were drinking from each other's bath water in a way.
The Hon. Member for Niagara Falls went on to say: "I suggest that leaving this in adds an element of uncertainty in the sentencing of an individual. No matter how despicable a polluter is, and we all agree that people who pollute are in a terrible category, one that should be punished, that person has the right to appeal to a higher court to see if the penalty is commensurate with that which is given in other Canadian jurisdictions. It is a principle of our law that when someone receives a penalty or a sentence, he has the right to appellate review to make sure there is not too great a disparity between similar cases".
These were words of a Member from the Niagara Peninsula where there has been such a head of steam built up over the years over environmental pollution. First of all, he entirely missed the point and, second, he did not understand what was the real intent of leaving in that very same clause his own Minister put into the Bill in the first place. That is beyond my understanding and it is very unfortunate that, at this stage, there is very little that can be done about it unless the Bill is sent back to committee for review.
I am moving quickly along. This Bill requires a much greater in-depth analysis than that which I have done. 1 want to draw the attention of Hon. Members to another aspect of the Bill that has been troublesome, and that is that we discovered with dismay in committee that when it comes to international air pollution, the Minister would apply, through this piece of legislation we are debating today, the concept of equivalency that he applied to toxic chemicals. That, of course, is not a desirable route to take.
The equivalency provisions, when applied to international air pollution, are in my view a step backward. To put on record the statements made about that by a number of organizations would take too long. The fact is that although we tried to correct the situation, we did not succeed. In this new Environmental Protection Act, we have now lost a measure which existed under the Clean Air Act, a measure which should exist, and that is the ability of enforcing and setting regulations that are of an international nature.
An analysis of the Bill as a whole leads to some general conclusions. One is that Bill C-74 can be put under the general heading of the mouse that roared. The Bill was heralded as a great measure. Expectations were raised. The draft Bill contained parts that were good and promising, and some of those parts were deleted after the consultations, without consulting again with interested parties except for the provinces. That is something that smacks of a procedural tactic which I do not like and of which I do not approve. I think it is a bad practice. It leaves with people the notion that somehow the Government has not dealt with them in a fair and honest manner.

April 26, 1988
Canadian Environmental Protection Act
If the Government consults, and then after consultation makes changes weakening or changing the direction of the document on which the Government has consulted, the least it would want to do in all honesty and good conscience is to let those people know by consulting them about the changes made to the document as it first existed. On those two counts, the raising of expectations and the consultation process, unfortunately I must say that the Government did not do well.
Second, the notion of the clean-up of the existing mess was raised on a number of occasions, particularly by the Minister, and in retrospect, this Bill will not be able to deliver. It is a step in the right direction of regulating chemicals in the market-place, but as such, the Bill will not clean up the existing pollution in the air, the water and the soil. Other measures, legislative or by way of programs, accords and joint action, will be required to do that.
In essence, we have here for third reading a piece of legislation which was written in part by the provinces and which gives to the provinces a say in the environment. This from a constitutional point of view, is tantamount to an abdication by the federal Government in an area in which it has full and clear jurisdiction. I would like to see this challenged and have the courts have a say on that at the appropriate time.
In reviewing this Bill, I see that there has also been a federal retreat on the environment. The Bill requires the Minister, under the equivalency provisions, to consult with this federal-provincial advisory committee prior to the making of regulations. This consultation is mandatory for regulations in areas where federal and provincial powers do overlap and areas that deal with the quantity or concentration of a toxic chemical that can be released, the places or areas where toxic chemicals may be released, the industrial activities that release toxic chemicals, the manner and conditions of releasing of toxic chemicals, the manner and conditions of storage, display, handling and transportation of toxic chemicals, and the disposal of toxic chemicals. Thus, in the key areas of the regulation of toxic chemicals, the federal Government has given up the right to make regulations under federal statute. It simply boils down to that, a surrender.
If a province wishes, it may opt out of the federal regulation proposed for a toxic chemical as defined by the Bill by way of an existing provincial regulation or by creating a new one that is deemed to be equivalent to the federal regulation. The new one need not be the same as, equal to or stronger than the federal regulation but equivalent to it, and that I must say does not mean it would be identical. Whatever that means, the bottom line of the equivalency provision is that the federal Government is abrogating its constitutional right and responsibility to regulate in the area of pollution and the environment. The equivalency provisions have seriously weakened the constitutional rights and responsibilities of the federal Government.
I would like to invite Hon. Members to examine a situation which might occur in the Province of Saskatchewan, let us say, which may find that the province bordering it to the East has
an equivalency provision in environmental protection regulations. Let us say that three years from now, there are no regulations in the Province of Saskatchewan. What guidelines or standards will the Government of Canada look at for use by the Province of Saskatchewan which may at that time have no regulations? Will it look to the East and borrow from Manitoba, or will it look to the West and borrow from Alberta? In fact, will it look to the North and borrow the standards of the Northwest Territories?
Most likely, when the federal Government sees it is forced to intervene and apply environmental protection regulations in a province where those regulations do not exist, it will apply the lowest standards available from a neighbouring province. It will have to do that politically because there will be an uproar by the provincial Government concerned, unless there is an unusually difficult and complex environmental situation where public opinion is aroused. That is what is going to happen and that is why the equivalency provisions are for the birds. This is an invasion of federal responsibility and a way of reducing the burden on the budget of the Department of the Environment and other Departments which may be involved in implementing this measure if the equivalency provisions had not been introduced last November.
Another serious flaw is that federal polluters can escape Bill C-74. You have heard me at length about that and I will not repeat myself, but the fact is that, having in a way created the appearance of wanting to prevent pollution by federal Departments and agencies, the Bill still contains a requirement for approval by a Minister other than the Minister of the Environment before you can stop the Bank of Canada, the National Research Council, CN's diesel engines, or any utility which may come under the jurisdiction of the federal Government, from polluting. This is a real cop-out. The individual is powerless. The individual or organization which could have been given the power to take action in the environment without being personally affected is not given that opportunity, despite the great declarations of the desirability of an environmental bill of rights by the Minister. The individual is powerless.
Then we have what I call the triumph of the coward, namely the deletion of the Subclause (g) that I referred to earlier. When the Bill was introduced last June it had a provision giving the Minister of the Environment the power to direct the polluter to pay for the cost of the investigation of a certain offence. It was a good provision because it can be very expensive to investigate crimes against the environment. None of the witnesses before the committee complained about that provision. Not even industry complained about it. However, when it came to clause-by-clause examination, the Hon. Member for Niagara Falls chose to move deletion of that clause because it was too "progressive and unprecedented". The Government then caved in, I suppose, and did not support reintroduction of that clause when we had the debate at report stage.
April 26, 1988

Finally, we have the fact that there are no national standards. In the draft Act released for public discussion in December, 1986, there was a reference to the responsibility of the federal Government to set national standards of environmental protection. It was there, it was good, it was hailed and supported. Then when Bill C-74 was given first reading in June of last year the standard had turned into "nationally consistent levels". What mush. What a cop-out. What a retreat.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: What a windbag.

You see the difference in those weaklings on the front benches who call themselves the Government of Canada. What a sham. What a disgrace. It is the responsibility of the Government of Canada to set national standards. It has the responsibility to guarantee to all Canadians this same degree of environmental protection from coast to coast.
Because of the equivalency provisions these very Tories here in this Chamber cannot guarantee national standards in the environment. The result of this policy will be a patchwork of environmental protection dependent on the degree of commitment of a province. When a province will not come through with its own set of regulations, the lowest common denominator will prevail and win the day. That is the philosophy of the Conservative Party of Canada, the lowest common denominator, the triumph of mediocrity.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased finally to have a chance to rise to speak at third reading on the Bill before us today. The Bill is certainly not all that it is claimed to be by the Minister. I am sorry he has perhaps had some second thoughts about it himself and has been too embarrassed to debate it at second reading or so far on third reading. I hope he will be along to face the music for a little bit on this question.
It has been called cradle-to-grave protection against and regulation of toxic chemicals. In a sense that is true but it is cradle-to-grave regulation of a very limited nature. It still remains the case that the approach to environmental protection under this Act is thoroughly inadequate.
We are going to approve this Act because it has some aspects that we want and which the environmental community have been asking for for a long time. We cannot say no at this stage. However, I am going to argue that when we look to the future we are going to have to do better.
I am going to be a little bit critical of the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia), the Liberal environment critic, because he has gone to town on the Conservative Government on this question. However, there are many places where he could have acted himself when he was Minister of the Environment. Some of the flaws in the Act we have before us now are similar to what is in the current legislation passed by a Liberal Government. Many of the things he could have been doing
Canadian Environmental Protection Act
when he talks about the need for an environmental Bill of rights the Liberal Government could have done. The Liberals were in government for a long time.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: With the help of the NDP.

The then Liberal Minister of the Environment, now the Liberal critic, could have instituted the very things of which he is criticizing the Conservatives. I will be critical of the Conservatives but I do not want anyone to think I am looking back to some golden past under a Liberal Government which was better than what we have with the Conservatives. That is simply not true either.
We have gone through report stage and extensive debate at third reading stage. Literally hundreds of amendments were proposed, but I am not going to go through them all. Simply by way of summary I will point out that some of the amendments brought forward to improve and strengthen the Act, the vast majority, were defeated by the Government. A number of amendments from myself and my NDP colleagues as well as the Liberal critic and other Conservative Members were accepted, but they tended to be relatively minor amendments. These did not change the thrust of the Bill. They did not really make it the tough Bill which Canadians are working for. They gave perhaps a little more to citizens' rights and a little more accountability in terms of what the Minister would do, but did not fundamentally change the thrust. I am sorry that I have to say that those defects still remain in the Bill.
This is essentially weak legislation. It is called the Canadian Environmental Protection Act, but Bill C-74 is much more modest in scope. It is really an update of the Environmental Contaminants Act, with some aspects of the Ocean Dumping Control Act and the Clean Air Act, and in some cases there has actually been a regression in protection, a weakening of the regulatory power. Not all of the changes have been in the direction of strengthening, although there has been some strengthening in the area of toxic chemicals.
Bill C-74 gives the Government the scope to identify toxic substances and the scope to regulate those toxic substances it had identified. It gives the Government the ability to screen new substances before they are used in the environment. Here we see the one fundamental improvement in the approach, the change in the onus of proof. Heretofore, industry could bring in anything it wanted and, in effect, after the fact people had to go to a great deal of trouble in order to prove that the substance was toxic and then some regulation would be brought in. In one scandalous case it took 10 years to get five toxic substances regulated, most of which were not being manufactured any more by that time in any event.

April 26, 1988
Canadian Environmental Protection Act
Industry will now have to convince regulators that the substance is safe to use. It will have to show the criteria used. Substances presently used can be put on to a priority list and tested. We have some means of redressing mistakes of the past. However, let us be very clear that this is a cumbersome and flawed process. It relies overwhelmingly on laboratory tests of various sorts. They deal with substances one at a time and do not take into effect the cumulative results of the different kinds of toxic contaminants. They do not consider what is happening in the environment.
These are lab tests in an unnatural environment, a controlled situation which does not exist in actual practice. They have completely separate regulations for pesticides and radioactive substances. The environment is being harmed by a variety of different sources which are regulated quite separately. It may be the cumulative effects of different components from various industrial, radioactive, and pesticide uses that will be really harmful. I do not think that we have adequate ways of investigating those kinds of effects yet.
Under the Environmental Protection Act Canadians will have the right to complain to the Government when substances are not identified or regulated to their satisfaction. In fact, we even had amendments in this case which reduced the number of people necessary to complain. We have facilitated the role of the public, which role we ought to be facilitating. Indeed, some of us would like to have this role extended because the public includes environmental groups, many of which are active in criticizing this Bill and in providing very helpful and constructive criticism and proposals for a different approach to this. There are concerned citizens with expertise who are a resource for the Government. We would want people to be extremely active in regulation and in alerting us to dangers. The more that can be done in this respect, the safer Canadians will be. The Government made some gestures in this direction and we are going in the right direction, but we could have gone further.
The Bill will ban the export of toxic substances, the use of which is banned in Canada. I was pleased that that amendment was accepted by the Government. If the substance is too toxic for us to be using, certainly we should not be exporting it to some other country which may have fewer resources to assess toxicity and which may be taken in by claims made and not in a strong position to carry out the tests which are, of course, enormously expensive, especially given the vast number of substances on the market.
The Bill will give the Government the right to regulate fuels on the basis of environmental quality. We were pleased to see that because emissions from motor vehicles are a prime source of pollution. They contribute to acid rain, among other things, and that is a significant improvement in the legislation. The Bill gives the Government regulatory authority over nutrients in water conditioners, another relatively minor matter but a step in the right direction.
The Bill will legislate federal authority over environmental matters with respect to federal lands and undertakings. I am sorry to say that further amendments to strengthen this aspect
of the Bill were rejected. Again, it is a question of moving in the right direction. It is an important and welcome move for the federal Government. One of the loopholes, curiously enough, was simply a lack of federal legislation on the environment, even in matters clearly under federal jurisdiction. This loophole is now being filled with the Environmental Protection Act.
Bill C-74 legislates governmental authority to make environmental regulations with respect to federal Departments and Crown agencies. This is, again, a very necessary step to take. One wonders why it has not been in place for a long time.
There is also a measure in this Bill to protect whistleblowers who report on breaches of government environmental regulations. I am very pleased to see this because we do have conscientious public servants who, from time to time, in a variety of Departments, find some practice which is weak and improper and may be flagrantly contrary to the laws and to regulations. We have had instances of public servants being fired for reporting on a practice which was quite wrong. The messenger of the bad news that the law was being broken was shot down instead of being welcomed and thanked for undertaking this public service and ensuring that the situation was remedied. There will now be protection for public servants who see breaches. I welcome this and hope that public servants will feel that they can be vigilant in carrying out their duties and not have to toe the line if someone is being slack in their Department.
The legislation gives the federal Government the authority to protect citizens of foreign countries from air pollution of Canadian origin. Most of our air pollution comes from the massive industry in the United States up to Canada. However, it can go the other way, and a small proportion does. It is quite right that Canadians provide adequate protection for the environment of our neighbours whom we may harm. I welcome these measures in the Bill.
The Bill establishes the possibility for boards of review to be created upon petition of individuals who are dissatisfied with regulations under the Act. This is another way in which people in voluntary organizations, academics, researchers, and other people involved in environmental work who see inadequacies in the regulations, can bring these inadequacies forward. There can be a form of petitioning and a board of review will be established in order to re-examine those regulations. We hope that the regulations would be strengthened accordingly if the case is made.
The Bill provides for very considerable fines, indeed up to SI million, for environmental crimes under the Act. In addition to fines, it provides for prison sentences of up to six months. The fines of up to $1 million are substantial, as they are intended to be. The prison sentences are quite modest, but they do exist. This is a clear sign to the Canadian public, to industry, to anyone who wishes to pollute, to anyone who can see that it will save them money to pollute by way of toxic chemicals, to people who are willing to sacrifice environmental health, the health of our people, and the health of our plant and animal life, that they will have to pay for it.
April 26, 1988

1 hope that these penalties will be an adequate dissuasion from pollution by way of toxic chemicals. This is a clear message that this kind of activity is extremely harmful. It can be more harmful than many crimes in the Criminal Code in terms of the impact. We do not know the full impact. We do not know the number of people who die from toxic contaminations of various sorts. We do not have this information. But we can be very sure that there are actual deaths and injuries, people are maimed, quality of life is disturbed, children are sickened. All of these kinds of things happen from industrial toxic chemicals that get into the environment and have a damaging effect either immediately or there are substances that are carcinogenic and which over time cause birth defects and impair people's enjoyment of life very substantially. These are crimes. They are profoundly wrong and harmful and need to be treated as such. Canadians have made the move. They want it to happen.
Bill C-74, however, does not do many things it ought to. It does not embrace many of the most destructive substances in use today. It excludes substances regulated by other Acts of Parliament despite the fact that the Minister has called this the most comprehensive piece of legislation. It is not a comprehensive piece of legislation. It excludes pesticides, no matter how toxic they are and, of course, it excludes nuclear contaminates no matter how toxic or dangerous they are. It is not comprehensive legislation. It is very narrowly focused.
It does not provide any standards of environmental quality. This is an issue which many of us made quite a bit of at committee stage and at report stage in the House. What we still have are guidelines. They are objectives. They are not as strong as standards that must be met. This is a serious deficiency in the Bill that remains.
The Government may, if it wishes, write guidelines or objectives or codes to suggest emission levels of substances in other aspect of environmental quality, but the Environmental Protection Act does not give Government the authority or the obligation to create the standards that would result in a cleaner environment. I would hope the Government would see the error of its ways and in the future would move to very clear standards.
The Bill does not incorporate a much demanded environmental bill of rights. We have instead merely a preamble at the front of the Bill which goes in that direction. We have a few provisions that allow for citizens to act at various stages, but it is not comprehensive. The Government has shied away from this. We are not entirely clear why. I want to make a few remarks about the jurisdictional question, which seems to be one reason the Government has failed to act. It wants to shove this matter off to the provinces and say that an environmental bill of rights could only be brought in by provincial Governments. That is extremely unfortunate. I am going to argue that we could be doing that at the federal level.
Canadians should have the right to healthy environment. There have been repeated demands to the Government to provide the clout, to give citizens the right to take polluters to
Canadian Environmental Protection Act
court, for example, citizens on behalf of future generations and on behalf of their children and their neighbours. That is not there. It is only if the person has a direct financial stake that he can take the polluter to court. In short, we still have a very narrow focus that pollution may cause some immediate harm that can be dealt with, but there is not the real understanding that pollution is harmful to everyone. We are all in this together. Pollution in one area will move to another. Underground rivers unite everyone. Toxic chemicals in one place will show up in another place by water or by air.
It is said that pesticides which are sprayed in a field in Alabama will turn up in the Great Lakes five days later. The winds carry toxic substances of various sorts. So it is extremely important that we have this more comprehensive approach, that we give citizens the right to act on behalf of the environment, to act on behalf of people who cannot speak, children, animals, the children of the future. We must see that environmental pollution is radically reduced and ultimately eliminated.
The Environmental Protection Act has not done anything on some of our major environmental issues. It is not addressing the issue of acid rain at all. It is not addressing the issue of the overuse of pesticides. It is not doing anything to replace polluting forms of energy with environmentally safe forms of energy. Of course, it does not address the issue of the nuclear industry at all. It does not address the issue of packaging and all the treatment of consumer products and the pollution which occurs there. This is a Bill that is really quite limited in scope, and when we look at the massive problems we have with the environment, we can see that this Bill is not taking us as far as it should.
The Bill does not put a time limit on how long Government can take to decide if a substance is toxic after being put on the priority list, to require Government to list a substance as toxic when its toxicity is established. This ought to be a requirement. We tried to get this built in, but the Government would not accept the amendments. Even when we have gone through the very cumbersome process of establishing the toxicity, the Government may be very slow to act. We do not have time limits to make it act more promptly.
There is no definition of equivalency in the Act or any criteria to describe carefully and precisely what would be required for the federal Government to relinquish the authority to regulate to the provinces. This is a matter about which many of us are extremely concerned. It means a weakening of federal authority, and we can have pollution ghettos as a result. The Government can relinquish the authority, or was planning to relinquish the authority to the provinces, under supposed equivalency provisions, but we do not know if the procedures, the processes or the standards brought in by the provinces will be truly equivalent because there is no firm definition, no criteria that says that established equivalency means precisely this and if it is not good enough then we will not accept it as equivalent. So we have the possibility of a serious weakening there.

April 26, 1988
Alternatives to Refrigerants
I think a very different approach to the environment is really needed. I want to point to some remarks made by a professor Ross Hume Hall in an article. Professor Hall has been extremely critical of this approach to the Act. I note the Liberal critic for the environment quoted Professor Hall as well. I want to point out that Professor Hall criticizes this Act, when he says that these are the same problems we have in the old Act, the Act of 1976. So here we have the irony of the Liberal critic quoting very favourably and seeming to agree with Professor Hall, yet the chief message of Professor Hall is that we are repeating the mistakes of the past. Whose mistakes? The mistakes made by the Liberal Government in its approach to environmental regulation.
What Professor Hall is saying is that things basically have not changed. We are not learning from our mistakes. The processes set up under the old Act were too cumbersome. They did not allow for adequate processing. We have the scandalous example of only five chemicals being banned in a period of ten years. This is a process under the old Act, under the Liberal Act. Now we have a new Act coming forward which even adds to the cumbersomeness of the process. It is not going to speed it up at all. It is still the same old Act.
Professor Hall says it is like having a bridge that is falling down and you hire the same architect and builder to rebuild the bridge. This is foolish. We would not do this if we were talking about bridges. But we are talking about the environment and somehow this Government has not got it through its head that the environment is at least as important as a bridge.
We have the Environment Contaminates Act of 1976. We have 60,000 industrial chemicals in Canada, 50,000 of which have never had any tests done as to their toxicity.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   THE ENVIRONMENT ADVISABILITY OF INTENSIFYING RESEARCH FOR ALTERNATIVES TO REFRIGERANTS
speechtext: When this motion was last before the House the Hon. Member for The Battlefords- Meadow Lake (Mr. Gormley) had the floor. Since he is not here, I will recognize the Hon. Member for Cowichan- Malahat-The Islands (Mr. Manly) on debate.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   THE ENVIRONMENT ADVISABILITY OF INTENSIFYING RESEARCH FOR ALTERNATIVES TO REFRIGERANTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak on this important motion put forward by the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia). I want to commend him for bringing this subject to the attention of the House. I urge all Hon. Members to familiarize themselves with the facts concerning chlorofluorocarbons, or CFCs as they are known, and the depletion of the ozone layer. This is a matter of life and death for our planet.
I said before in this House that the crisis in the environment has created a crisis in our system of parliamentary democracy. Unless we can find some way of dealing with the crisis in the environment, then our system of parliamentary democracy is under threat by some sort of totalitarian government that might perhaps offer the promise of being able to deal with environmental crises. Today being the second anniversary of the Chernobyl disaster, I think we should remind ourselves that totalitarian governments do not have any better track record in dealing with environmental questions than do parliamentary democracies.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   THE ENVIRONMENT ADVISABILITY OF INTENSIFYING RESEARCH FOR ALTERNATIVES TO REFRIGERANTS
speechtext: Not as well.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   THE ENVIRONMENT ADVISABILITY OF INTENSIFYING RESEARCH FOR ALTERNATIVES TO REFRIGERANTS
speechtext:
Not as well, perhaps. But the situation is that parliamentary democracies do not have a good track record. Unless we develop a better track record, we are under some threat because there will be the possibility, the appeal, that some other system might have that could manage the environment better. It is incumbent on Members on all sides of the House to deal with this situation, and with all environmental questions, in a much more serious and intelligent manner than we have done so far.
Like the crisis in the environment, the crisis in democracy is not something that can be seen immediately. However, it is insidious and the long-term effects are devastating. Simply put, the continuing degradation of the environment, the poisoning of our oceans, our lakes, our rivers, the destruction of the tropical forests and, indeed, forests in temperate regions of Canada, desertification, acid rain, the destruction of the ozone layer and the stratosphere constitute as much of a threat to human survival as nuclear war. Indeed, nuclear war itself threatens the form of environmental degradation that puts it into a different category from all previous kinds of war. It is the environmental threat of nuclear war that makes it qualitatively different from all other kinds of war because it threatens to destroy the basis on which human life is able to continue on this planet.
April 26, 1988

The crisis for democracy lies in the fact that we are so slow to recognize threats to our environment. When we do recognize these threats we seem even slower to act. While we wait to act, the silent destruction of our world continues.
If we are slow to move in this House, we are even more slow to move at the international level. Vested interests of large corporations and questions of national sovereignty seem to take precedence over our common future as members of a common family which wants to keep on living on this planet. On September 19, commenting on the Montreal Protocol, GWynne Dyer pointed out that it took 10 years to reach this Protocol which calls for a 50 per cent cut in CFCs by 1999, when scientists have said that what we need is a 85 per cent cut in CFC production and use immediately. Dyer pointed out that the total annual value of CFC production in industry is only about $1 billion, a comparatively small sum when we look at some of the vested interests in some other industries that are also polluting our world. If we have that much trouble regulating an industry that is worth $1 billion, how much more difficult is it to regulate international industries that mount up into the billions upon billions of dollars?
It is important that we understand the importance of the ozone layer to human life on this planet. The ozone layer and the stratosphere filter ultraviolet radiation B. The depletion of this ozone layer increases the risk of skin cancer in human beings. Scientists have estimated that a 1 per cent loss of ozone translates directly into a 4 per cent increase in the risk of skin cancer. Already, Canadians face a 15 per cent increase in skin cancer because of the loss of ozone that has already taken place.
We can also look at the effect of ozone on the protection that it gives to world food crops. Wheat, corn, rice and soybeans are all sensitive to ultraviolet radiation B. Again, a 1 per cent loss of ozone can translate into a 1 per cent loss in soy production. Phytoplankton, the base of the aquatic food chain, is also affected negatively by ultraviolet radiation. Therefore, it depends on the protection that is given it by the ozone layer.
Given the importance of the ozone layer to human life, and to all life on this planet, we need to recognize that anything that threatens the ozone layer has to be regarded as an enemy of human life. This is precisely what chlorofluorocarbons do.
CFCs are stable synthetics that were developed in the 1930s originally as refrigerants. They are now used as blowing agents in the production of rigid foams, as propellants in aerosols and as cleaners for microchips. When released, these fairly static elements are carried slowly up into the atmosphere and beyond into the stratosphere, taking as long as five years before they get up to the area where the ozone layer is. Then, they are broken down by the intense energy of the sun. A single chlorine atom released from the breakdown of these CFCs can break down 10,000 ozone molecules.
The stability of these compounds means that they last anywhere from 60 to 300 years before they break down. An
Alternatives to Refrigerants
average life would be around 100 years. In other words, there is a very long lead time before they come fully into effect. They constitute a ticking time bomb. Since there is an annual increase of about 6 per cent or 7 per cent of the amount of CFCs that are released into the stratosphere, and since they only break down at most at a rate of 1 per cent per year, there is a gradual cumulative build-up of these ticking time bombs that are eating away at the ozone layer.
It has been estimated that CFC production and use would have to be reduced by 85 per cent to bring our system back into balance. Even this 85 per cent reduction would not restore the ozone layer to its original condition.
The Montreal Protocol agreed to last fall was an important first step. If ratified, it would lead by a series of phased reductions to a 50 per cent reduction by June 30, 1999 in production and use of CFCs. It is a small step. We need to go further.
The motion that has been put forward by the Hon. Member for Davenport refers specifically to refrigerants, which, as he points out, is the largest of all CFC use in Canada. It calls for intensified research for alternatives.
I believe that this motion is politically realistic. Even though CFCs need to be identified as life threatening, it is not possible to ban them completely even in Canada let alone in other parts of the world. They are too damn convenient for us all. Thus there is a need to step up the search for alternatives.
I urge all Members to accept this motion. I urge the Government to pay attention to it.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   THE ENVIRONMENT ADVISABILITY OF INTENSIFYING RESEARCH FOR ALTERNATIVES TO REFRIGERANTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak to this motion. The House now knows all the facts, and our conclusion must be that all groups in our society share a responsibility to protect the ozone layer. Government, industry and consumers share a common point: we are all individuals who live on this planet and who each have a definite interest in protecting a vital element of their environment.
The Government, Mr. Speaker, sets a very high priority on dealing with the problem of the destruction of the ozone layer and its impact on our climate. I may remind the House of the key role played by Canada in drafting two international agreements on protecting the ozone layer. In 1986, Canada became the first country to ratify the Vienna Convention for the Protection of the Ozone Layer. The Convention establishes a framework for international co-operation in research and information exchange. Today, 16 of the required number of ratifications, which is 20, have already been received by the United Nations Environment Program, and three more are expected shortly.

April 26, 1988
Alternatives to Refrigerants
Last September, Canada, together with 23 other countries and the European Economic Community, signed the Montreal Protocol on substances that deplete the ozone layer. Since then, six more countries have signed this agreement. I may remind the House that it was in recognition of Canada's efforts that the United Nations Environment Program accepted Canada's offer to host the diplomatic conference in Montreal.
Mr. Speaker, the Montreal Protocol is the first national agreement that is actually a tool for managing environmental problems, since it provides an international framework for responding to such problems before they reach the crisis stage. The parties must meet specific objectives for the consumption of control substances. Consumption, defined as production plus imports minus exports, is thus substituted for the term emissions. Every party to the Protocol will have to reduce its consumption of CFCs to that of 1986, and do so by 1990. It will have to do the same with respect to halon levels by 1992. This initial step will be followed by two more, and by 1999, consumption of CFCs must be half what it was in 1986. The Department of the Environment is developing a series of options for freezing and reducing consumption, in accordance with the requirements of the Protocol. A report describing these options will be released within the next few weeks to gauge public response.
Mr. Speaker, recent scientific discoveries show that the international community must speed up its efforts to reduce the emissions of substances that erode the ozone layer, even beyond what is required by the Montreal Protocol, if we are really to stop the destruction of ozone. For this purpose, Environment Canada is considering additional regulations that will take Canada beyond the reduction targets set in the Protocol. Such regulations can include a requirement to put in place codes of technical recommendations for some use sectors that need modern technology to reduce emissions through recycling. Similarly, a ban or other restriction on frivolous uses or on products containing regulated substances, a product labeling program or any other innovative idea that may come up during the regulatory development phase.
Internationally, the Government intends to continue promoting the early implementation of the Montreal Protocol. I remind the House that implementation requires ratification by 11 states representing two-thirds of total 1986 production of controlled substances. To date, only the United States and Mexico have ratified this agreement. The European Economic Community and Japan are expected to ratify it shortly. Canada, for its part, intends to ratify it as soon as the Canadian Environmental Protection Act receives Royal Assent.
Mr. Speaker, if all these nations ratify as soon as expected, the requirements for the Protocol to take effect will be met and the Montreal Protocol will come into force on January 1, 1989. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has made known his intention to put the subject of the ozone layer on the agenda at
the next economic summit in Toronto in June. I am confident that all Hon. Members will agree that this is appropriate.
Mr. Speaker, all the initiatives that I have just described to you are but a reflection of this Government's intention to find a solution to this world-wide ecological problem. Industry is somewhat more in agreement that the long-term solution lies in environmentally safe substitutes.
Excited with the idea of a multi-billion dollar market, industry has already committed itself to an aggressive research program to develop alternatives as quickly as possible. In many cases, companies have not hesitated to pool their resources to carry out toxicological studies or to accelerate production technology for the most promising substitutes.
I am very encouraged by the recent response from the world's largest CFC producer to the concerns raised by the scientific discoveries that I described a few minutes ago. Not only is the international giant Du Pont encouraging all nations to speed up the ratification of the Montreal Protocol, but it has also set itself the goal of completely discontinuing CFC production. I must applaud such a move since it is the first time that industry recognizes a direct link between the destruction of ozone and CFCs.
Mr. Speaker, obviously, a government publication on substitutes would not be appropriate at this time. We must leave funding for such research to those who will reap substantial rewards from marketing environmentally safe substitutes. Nevertheless, this position does not prevent the Government from following the issue of research very closely and acting if necessary.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would tell the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) that although the Government cannot support his motion, it nevertheless thanks him for bringing the matter to the attention of the House. I express the wish that all parties will show the same co-operation in future efforts to resolve the problem of the destruction of the ozone layer and thus ensure a healthy atmosphere for future generations.
Mr. Speaker, it is gratifying to see that already some companies like Provigo in Quebec have announced that they are trying to eliminate all chlorofluorocarbon-based products from their shelves as quickly as possible. That is encouraging. Some companies like Du Pont, corporations that are already distributing products, have followed the Government's lead and I think, Mr. Speaker, that it is very promising for the future of this country and especially of planet Earth.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   THE ENVIRONMENT ADVISABILITY OF INTENSIFYING RESEARCH FOR ALTERNATIVES TO REFRIGERANTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in the continuing debate on this motion. I am thankful that the debate is coming to a close. I think that all Hon. Members have the facts before them to be able to vote authoritatively on this subject.
April 26, 1988

Let me begin my brief intervention by quoting from one voice of concern, my 16-year-old son, Liam. When I told him last night that I would be participating in a debate on this most important subject, and asked him for his thoughts, Liam said: "If the ozone layer is ever destroyed, we'd all get fried". Then he added: "I can't believe people would ever ignore something which is so necessary for our very existence. But it's true, no one cares or even thinks about using aerosol cans. They don't care diddly-squat about the ozone layer".
There you have it, Mr. Speaker, that is what the present generation of young adults think about how we, the present rulers of industry, Government, and the country tend to regard this critical matter raised by my hon. friend.
Yet, using my son's words as a text, this debate pinpoints the responsibility that we all share as consumers, together with Government and industry, to protect the ozone layer for the future well-being of our planet, and for Liam's generation and beyond.
My son points out the responsibility that we all share as consumers. This Government is at present engaged in a number of activities to generate initiatives aimed at bringing about a solution to this problem as quickly as possible, both on the domestic front and the international front. In that connection, let me pay tribute to Canada's Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) and his very able Parliamentary Secretary, the Hon. Member for Scarborough Centre (Mrs. Browes). In my view, both the Minister and his Parliamentary Secretary, along with Members on both sides of the House, are extremely concerned about this very critical threat to the future of this planet. We are working on all fronts to establish a solution to this global problem. We have heard about the activities and initiatives of Environment Canada in respect of the development and implementation of a domestic control program aimed at reducing the emission of ozone-depleting chemicals.
In October of 1986, the National Aeronautics and Space Administration, NASA, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, NOAA, the Federal Aviation Administration, FAA, the World Meteorological Organization, WMO, and the United Nations Environment Program, UNEP, formed an ozone trends panel that involved more than 100 scientists from around the world. This panel, which included scientists from the Atmospheric Environment Service of Environment Canada, was established to study the question of whether carefully re-evaluated ground-based data and satellite data would support the model predictions. The conclusions of that panel, reported in the spring of 1988, revealed that there is undisputed observational evidence of atmospheric concentrations of source gases important in controlling stratospheric ozone levels, including chlorofluorocarbons, halons, methane, nitrous oxide, and carbon dioxide, all of which continue to increase on a global scale as a result of the activities of humans. There has also been a large, sudden, unexpected decrease in the abundance of spring time Antarctic ozone over the last decade.
Alternatives to Refrigerants
The total column of ozone in the austral spring of 1987 at all latitudes south of 60 degrees south was the lowest since measurements began 30 years ago!
Many of these same scientists have reached the conclusion that global emissions of chlorofluorocarbons, or CFCs, and halons, need to be reduced by in excess of 85 per cent in order to reduce the rate of depletion of the ozone layer.
Our scientists have warned us that increasing concentrations of CFCs and halons, both of which are very efficient infrared radiation absorbers, in the atmosphere will contribute significantly to increasing the earth's temperature over the coming years to a level which has not existed for millions of years! This is frightening stuff.
They tell us that we are already committed to a significant global warming, and they are calling the accelerated change in the climate of our planet "potentially catastrophic".
These effects are predicted to occur in a manner and at a rate that makes the future sound like some sort of long-running science fiction horror movie. We will face rising sea levels, with the consequent submergence of coastal communities such as Prince Edward Island; changes in the location of deserts; extremely high temperatures in cities during the summer months-as if they weren't high enough already; an increase in the number and severity of hurricanes; and the death of a significant quantity of the world's forests.
These recent scientific findings signal a warning to the world's political institutions: the continuing depletion of the ozone layer must be effectively arrested. We must hear about the response of this Government and industry to these findings.
This Government is committed to effective ozone layer protection, and it is prepared to back up that commitment with concrete action.
Let me turn for a moment to the role of the consumer in the resolution of this problem, because the power of the consumer is paramount. For some years I was the consumer affairs critic for our Party, and I know that if a consumer does not want to buy, the product will not survive in the market-place.
Regulations prohibiting the use of CFCs as propellants in certain aerosols, notably hairsprays, deodorants and antipers-pirants, were put in place in 1980 pursuant to the Environmental Contaminants Act, and that came about as a direct result of pressure from consumers.
Reduced Canadian consumption of CFCs dropped to about one-half of the 1974 peak level. But the success was temporary. Since that time, consumption levels have again reached the peak levels of 1974, all due to the substantial growth in unregulated uses. Once again, alarmed Canadian consumers are voicing their strong concerns about the continued production and use of ozone-depleting CFCs and halons. Many are calling for a variety of measures to control the problem, including a complete ban on the use of CFCs and halons, the mandatory labelling of products, and a boycott of some forms of plastic foam packaging made with CFCs.

April 26, 1988
Adjournment Debate
Last August, McDonald's announced its plans to phase out the use of plastic foam packaging made with CFCs. More recently, Provigo, a major chain food and convenience stores in the Province of Quebec, announced its intention to follow suit.
So, consumers' influence can be used to facilitate the switch to non-ozone-depleting consumer products. Driven by these express consumer preferences and the substantial market incentives emerging therefrom, industry has mounted a major research program to develop and market environmentally safe substitutes for all uses of CFCs. Environment Canada has developed, and will be implementing in the very near future, a control strategy to deal with the depletion of the ozone layer.
In conclusion, industry must begin now to plan for cutting back consumption of CFCs, regardless of whether they produce, use, import or export controlled chlorofluorocarbons. In order to provide an enhanced level of protection for the ozone layer, Canada will implement additional control measures. Toward that end, a report will be circulated for consultation and discussion later this summer.
As is apparent, this Government is clearly committed to the resolution of this problem. This Government is fully prepared to consider involvement in research, should areas be identified in the future where the Government can play a role.
Mr. Speaker, the facts bearing on this issue speak for themselves, and for generations to come.

subtopic: ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS-APPLICABILITY OF PROVINCIAL LAW TO FEDERAL AGENCIES
ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS-APPLICABILITY OF PROVINCIAL LAW TO FEDERAL AGENCIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, have you ever received a parking ticket? Don't feel badly, because virtually everyone in this country has had a parking ticket from time to time. I have had parking tickets myself and friends of mine have had parking tickets.
One of my friends whom I recall very vividly was an old law school classmate of mine, a fellow by the name of Jack Pinkofsky. Jack and I went to law school in Toronto. We attended Osgoode Hall Law School when Osgoode Hall was in downtown Toronto. Just to the north of it was a piece of property on which was located the old University Avenue Armouries. Jack used to park on the boulevard of that armoury property. You are right, Mr. Speaker, the University Avenue Armouries was torn down some years ago and the new Toronto court-house was built on that property. When the old University Avenue armouries was there, Jack Pinkofsky used to park his car every day on the boulevard of the University Avenue Armouries. As you can expect, Mr. Speaker, anyone who parks on such a boulevard gets a parking ticket, especially when parking all day and where there is a sign which quite clearly says that you cannot park there at any time. Jack got several parking tickets. The police got after him and he was taken to court on one ticket.
April 26, 1988

Jack was an ingenious sort of guy, and he still is. He decided to fight the ticket, and he fought it on some very interesting grounds. He argued that the ticket was based on a municipal by-law; that the municipal by-law was passed under the authority of a provincial law; and that, in fact, the armouries property stood on federal property, not an provincial property. Therefore, municipal by-laws authorized by provincial laws did not apply to federal property.
The courts found that Jack was right and that federal property was immune from any law passed by the Province of Ontario, or authorized and passed by a municipality. Jack did not have to pay his parking ticket. He got off not because he was not parking there illegally but because of a technicality.
The Jack Pinkofsky situation is the same sort of situation which the federal Government ran into recently when a federal polluter was charged under the Province of Ontario's environmental laws with breaking those laws, being in breach of them, and thus subject to all the harsh penalties for which the Ontario environmental laws provide.
What happened in that case? We find that in the federal Department of Justice there are some ingenious people like Jack Pinkofsky and that in fact they fought and defended that case, not on the grounds that this particular federal polluter had not broken provincial law, not on the grounds that this federal polluter was not a polluter, but on the technical grounds that in fact provincial laws did not apply to federal polluters. That is the sort of defence used not only by Jack Pinkofsky with parking tickets but now by the federal Justice Department with federal polluters.
I do not know about you, Mr. Speaker, but I do not think that a federal polluter should be able to get off on technical grounds like that. It is one thing for a parking ticket, but it is an entirely different thing for something severe like that.
Fortunately the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) agreed with us. In answer to a question I put to him in the House he said that he felt that the new Canadian Environmental Protection Act would apply to all federal polluters and that there would be no problem with that sort of situation. Unfortunately that is not really the case.
In fact the Minister realized that and said that he would be prepared to see the legislative committee dealing with this matter actually put forward some amendments to change the Bill and to ensure that any federal polluter who actually breached the law would be convicted and penalized as a result of that breach.
Of course the Parliamentary Secretary knows that the legislative committee dealing with the Environmental Protection Act went through a great process. Over 300 amendments were put and many were accepted. The Parliamentary Secretary who is here tonight played an outstanding role on
Adjournment Debate
that committee, as did the Minister, and I have nothing but praise for the process. Unfortunately it left something to be desired in the area of whether or not a federal polluter would be quite clearly subject to and penalized by this Act and by federal pollution laws.
Clauses 52 and 53 of the Bill leave something to be desired-
