speakeroldname: Mrs. Pauline Browes (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
subtopic: ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS-APPLICABILITY OF PROVINCIAL LAW TO FEDERAL AGENCIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, thank you for providing me an opportunity to respond to my colleague from the great riding of York East, my neighbour in Metro Toronto. I am pleased to respond to the Hon. Member's question on the matter of enforcement of environmental legislation concerning federal polluters. Indeed, just today, we have been debating Bill C-74, the Bill in question.
There has been concern expressed that Bill C-74 did not bind the Crown. That fear, in the Government's view, is groundless. Clause 4 of the Bill states that the Canadian Environmental Protection Act is "binding on Her Majesty in right of Canada or of a province". This means that the statute is binding on the Government of Canada and on both provincial and territorial Governments.
The only circumstance in which it could be argued that the aforementioned might not be true is an offence by a federal Department, agency, board, or Crown corporation where a province or territory is enforcing its own regulation recognized through an Order in Council under the Canadian Environmental Protection Act as equivalent to requirements of the federal Act.
The Government is indebted to a lawyer for an environmental law group, the Canadian Environmental Law Association, for pointing out this deficiency. The Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) urged the legislative committee charged with the clause-by-clause review of Bill C-74 to make the necessary amendments to close the loophole, and the committee did so.
On repeated occasions the Minister has declared his concern that federal Departments, agencies, boards, and Crown corporations must not be above the law when the environment is at stake. The committee of which the Hon. Member himself was an outstanding member and contributed a great deal was of the same mind. It made further amendments to Bill C-74 to ensure that no longer will there be any doubt on the matter.

April 26, 1988
Adjournment Debate
The revamped Bill now empowers the Government, on recommendation of the Minister of the Environment, to make regulations setting limits for emissions and effluents released by federal Departments, agencies, boards, and Crown corporations. Waste handling and disposal can also be regulated. It further requires that if a harmful substance has been released into the environment, the federal body which had management, charge or control of the substance immediately prior to its unauthorized release must report to an inspector or other designated person. That body must then take all reasonable emergency measures to prevent danger to the environment, human life or health, and to notify members of the public who may be adversely affected.
Bill C-74 now specifically indicates that inspectors have the right of access and entry to federal property and may take emergency measures if the relevant federal Department, board, agency, or Crown corporation fails to do so.
With the amended provisions in place-and there were a number of them-the Minister can now set about developing regulations to ensure that activities of federal Departments, agencies, boards, and Crown corporations do not pollute what we recognize as Canada's most precious resource, its environment. The concerns of the Hon. Member have been met in the amended Bill C-74 now before the House.
APPROVAL OF PROJECT/REQUEST THAT PROJECT PROCEED

Mr. Speaker, I should like to address tonight the whole issue of household garbage collecting and recycling process. My question in the House to the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mrs. McDougall) had to do with an application from a Quebec group from Lotbiniere, more specifically from Victoriaville, for support in a development of its household garbage collecting and recycling program. The Minister of Employment and Immigration wants to know whether it was a job creation or conservation project. Well, it is both. It is a household garbage collecting and recycling project for environmental purposes, which also aims at preserving jobs, because jobs have been created in Victoriaville, in Bois-Francs, for this recuperation demonstration program. There are about 25 people working there full-time, including a number of unskilled workers who, without these jobs, would be on welfare. So these are good, wholesome, permanent community jobs. Our purpose is not to send people to look for jobs in other regions, but to create jobs in our own area by using recoverable household garbage.
I have also visited "Cascades" in the Lotbiniere region, a private corporation which is using recycled paper. Now, in Canada, we are using only 20 per cent recycled paper. In Europe, they use as much as 60 per cent. They are much more advanced in Europe. It is much better for the environment to use recycled paper. Why? Because the pulp and paper making process results in the pollution of our rivers and lakes, because of the detrimental effects of chlorine on water and the
production of dioxins. Recycled paper avoid these negative effects on the environment by re-using paper.
There was a whole lot of correspondance on this subject. An application was sent to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) who referred it to the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) but the Department of Environment could not provide funds for this Bois-Francs Recuperation et Recyclage project. So an application was sent to the Minister of Employment and Immigration who replied that it was not the responsibility of her Department. What we need is a collecting and recycling policy, because it would be better for the environment and for job creation. We need a policy which would take the environment, investment, the prices of recycled products into account, as well as the need to create full-time jobs within the community.
We now have those projects, but the problem exists. For example, Bois-Francs has experienced an increased demand for recycling from municipalities. Well, this means that more products and waste are carried to dumps. The price of recycled products has gone down because there is not enough demand from manufacturers for them. A fine national project is in financial trouble as a result of decreased demand. What should be done? We have to promote demand and tax non-recycled products. There is the possibility among others that a satisfactory policy to encourage recovery and recycling would be to make more costly the refusal to use those recycled products.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, this is a very good enterprise. It is extremely encouraging and is employing people. It could expand its educational work, its work in the municipalities, to ensure that even more jobs are created. They would be good jobs in the community.
What response have we received?

As stated by the Minister of the Environment, in reply to Bois-Francs: "The recovery and recycling of waste contribute to the economic development of regions by creating jobs and reducing the use of natural resources". The activities of the industrial sector also contribute to reduce environmental problems affecting urban centres and to improve the management of domestic waste.
It is quite clear that those two objectives are aimed at and can be attained with a satisfactory financing of recovery and recycling. The Government should review that basic issue and promote a real policy for recovery, protection of the environment and creation of jobs.

speakeroldname: Mr. Benno Friesen (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to answer on behalf of the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mrs. McDougall). I would first like to point out that there are at least six streams in the Canadian Jobs Strategy and that it involves probably thousands of projects across Canada.
April 26, 1988

If the Hon. Member had really been interested in a fulsome explanation from the Minister on that day, it would have been helpful for her to have given notice to the Minister so that he could have been briefed on the details of this application. Even the Member, who has an encyclopaedic knowledge of Canada and of everything going on in Canada, would agree that the Minister cannot, on a day-to-day basis, be totally briefed on every project in Canada.
You've had weeks now to respond.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext:
And I will respond. I suggest that the Hon. Member may not have been searching for a fulsome answer, that there may have been some politics involved.
The Member has raised an environmental question and has praised the quality of this application. Neither I nor the Minister would quarrel with the quality of the project or the application. However, the Member is a well educated person; she has had extensive university training. If, during the course of her pursuit for her economics degree, she had applied for a scholarship toward economics in the fine arts department, she would have probably been told that it was a great application but that she was in the wrong department. Therefore I suggest to the Member that talking about quality of the project really is not the question before us.
But it is creating jobs.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext: The question is: Does it follow the criteria? While we all agree that the project the Member has promoted is a good one, it does not fall within the criteria. It does not help for her to say that the Minister should stop sending it around. Actually, the project came to the attention of the Department in April, 1987. It responded to the proposal on April 16, 1987 and again in June, 1987. It is pretty hard for the Member to say that it has been simply sent around the Department. Actually the Member brought it to the attention of the House on March 8, 1988, whereas the Hon. Member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Tremblay) has been working on this project for a year and a half-
Without success. Where is the funding?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip's assistant; Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subtopic: FINANCE-REFORM OF LEGISLATION-CONSEQUENCE FOR MOUVEMENT DESJARDINS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on April 15, 1988, I briefly expressed to the Minister of State (Finance) (Mr. Hockin) my concern about this Government's legislation dealing with trust and loan companies.
As you certainly can imagine, Mr. Speaker, I put that question because of the possible implications for the Mouve-ment Desjardins.
As you know, Mouvement Desjardins alltogether is one of the most important, if not the single most important financial co-operative group in Canada.
Its assets are nearly $31 billion. This means it is very important to hear Desjardins's considerations in this process.
When I myself analyse the trust company legislation, I hardly see how Desjardins and its group of companies would be exempted from the new requirements that would be imposed upon trust and loan companies by the legislation.
Indeed, I believe that when administering the legislation, bureaucrats could view the Desjardins group as a corporation, although the Desjardins group is a huge financial co-op.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, the legislation's intent is to prevent conflicts of interests within small groups of companies with business links, which conflicts could in some cases lead to some stockholders catering to their own needs at the expense of investors, consumers.

April 26, 1988
Adjournment Debate
That legislation is aimed at preventing inequities that could harm consumers and investors, which is both just and reasonable.
However, Desjardins is not a corporation. Under its structure, that institution is for all pratical purposes completely protected from conflicts of interests. Here is why, Mr. Speaker.
There are no small groups at Desjardins. Desjardins belongs to 4,200,000 shareholders. In Quebec, one out of five of every man, woman and child is a Desjardins shareholder.
The development strategy of Desjardins is determined by 18,330 volunteer directors, working together with a team of 28,500 Desjardins employees.
Mr. Speaker, if a conflict of interest were found in the growth of the Desjardins group, it would affect all Quebecers.
For all these reasons, speaking as the Member for the riding where Desjardins himself was born and where the headquarters are located, and considering the significance of this immense financial co-operative movement, of a tool whose continued growth is essential to Quebecers, I would ask you to further clarify this proposed legislation. I agree with the objective which is to protect Canadians who depend on trust and loan companies, but it should not, for want of definition and clarity-and that is what is important-be detrimental to the continued growth of the collective property of 20 per cent of the population of Quebec.
Sir, 1 thank you, and I trust your decision.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to apologize to the Hon. Member for Levis (Mr. Fontaine). From time to time in the House we finish our business a little earlier than anticipated. The Hon. Member has good reason to expect a response from the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Vincent). However, he is not with us today because of the change in time. If we had gone on to the "Late Show" at the normal time, 1 am sure he would have been here. However, 1
will do my best to provide a response on behalf of the Government to the Hon. Member.

In the House, Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Levis has a reputation for being a good MP and he always represents his electors' interests passionately and also intelligently.
But regarding the Mouvement Desjardins, he has a reputation that perhaps goes beyond this House and into the community as well. He always defends the interests of the Mouvement Desjardins in this House, in committee and in his community too, I think.

It is that kind of intelligent and compassionate approach which ensures that any piece of legislation brought forward to the House is examined with thoroughness and skill to ensure that the legislation will do good things on behalf of the people in the movement and on behalf of the communities which are involved, as well as with the co-operative. I am sure interventions he has already made in this Chamber, as well as the interventions he has made directly to the Minister and the interventions which will come as the legislation is introduced and moved forward to committee, will be reason for the people connected to this movement to feel confident that nothing in the legislation will do them harm. Indeed, the legislation will facilitate the movement and will facilitate the strength and capacity of Canadians to dream and to care about their children, their communities, and their standard of living.
That is the best I can do on short notice, Mr. Speaker, but I feel it sincerely. This Member is one Member of the House who approaches things, does not forget, and keeps working on them in order that they come out right and are helpful.
